ruststream-sqs-sns is the Amazon SQS broker for RustStream, built on the official aws-sdk-sqs client. A service reads and writes SQS queues, and with the sns feature it also publishes to SNS topics. The guides take an SQS service from installation to production. Start with Getting started.
This section draws how SQS and SNS work, where ruststream-sqs-sns sits between them and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs a service.

How ruststream-sqs-sns measures itself: the three loops, the run on an SQS endpoint, the broker-bound arithmetic and the code count. The procedure is the framework's own (RustStream methodology), and this page states what it is on SQS.

One process runs each scenario three times over, as three loops that differ in one thing: what carries the messages. Raw client. aws-sdk-sqs, driven directly: receive ten messages per call, decode each one, delete each one. One receive stays in flight while the loop settles the batch it holds, as this crate's pump does. Broker crate. This crate and nothing above it: the broker connects, the SqsQueue descriptor opens a subscription, and a loop pulls deliveries off its stream, decodes them and acks them. RustStream. The service a user writes: a #[subscriber] handler and the app around it. Everything else is equal across the three: the AWS configuration, the 25-second attempt timeout, the receive of ten messages with a 20-second wait, a DeleteMessage per message, the decode into the same struct, the body bytes, the tokio runtime with four worker threads, and the binary. The body is 512 bytes of JSON. It decodes into a struct of two integer fields, so the decode allocates nothing and the number is about this crate rather than about the JSON parser.

A fresh queue per run. The queue is created before the run and deleted after it, so a run never sees what an earlier one left. The consumer attaches first. Eight publishers then fill the queue, one SendMessage per message, and stay at most 4096 messages ahead of the consumer. The window opens at the first delivery and closes when the last one is handled, in all three loops. Creating the queue, building the clients and opening the subscription are outside it. The message count comes from a probe, which measures the raw loop's rate, so a measured run lasts at least five seconds on any machine. The loops are interleaved: raw, crate, RustStream, three rounds. Each loop reports its best, median and worst round. A row is broker-bound when round trips to the endpoint account for at least half of the time a delivery took. That is arithmetic. A probe times the smallest request the endpoint answers, on a client of its own, over 2000 calls. A delivery costs one round trip for its DeleteMessage and a tenth of the ReceiveMessage that carried its batch. The row is flagged when their product reaches half the measured time per message. The round trip is published with the machine, so the arithmetic can be checked.

Each scenario of the cost chart is the service a user writes, on SqsBroker against the same endpoint, built without the testing feature and started on a single-threaded runtime. Another thread fills the queue before the measured region opens, and that thread is not counted. Instructions come from callgrind and allocations from DHAT. A scenario runs over one delivery, then 1000, then 2000. The difference between the last two is the steady cost of a message, and the single delivery is the cold start. The count covers everything the service's thread runs: the runtime, this crate and the AWS SDK with its HTTP stack. Threads the SDK runs on its own are not counted, and neither is the endpoint's side of a round trip. Four runs of one binary agree within half a percent on instructions, because how the endpoint answers and how the socket's reads split move a little between runs. A run against a saved baseline fails on two percent more instructions in a scenario. Allocations are held to a floor each scenario declares, the highest count observed plus a tenth of a percent, on every run.

just bench The recipe starts the LocalStack stand from docker-compose.test.yml, runs both comparison scenarios, stops the stand and rewrites docs/benchmarks/results.json. It takes a few minutes and wants the machine to itself. It clears RUSTFLAGS, so the binary is not tied to the CPU it was built on. Both recipes build the benchmarks the way a release is built, with fat link-time optimization across crates, so the numbers describe the code a service ships. just bench-code The code count takes a few minutes and needs valgrind. just bench-code 5000 measures every scenario over five thousand deliveries instead of a thousand. just bench-code --save-baseline=main on main records a baseline, and just bench-code --baseline=main on a branch compares with it.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-sqs-sns measure, and what they do not allow you to conclude.

The three loops of a row are comparable with each other, because they ran in one process, interleaved, against one endpoint. A row is not comparable with a row another broker crate publishes: the transports do different work per message. Every message costs an HTTP round trip of its own, the DeleteMessage behind its ack. Those round trips set the pace of both rows. In a broker-bound row they took at least half of the time a delivery took. The work of the crate and the runtime then happens inside a wait the raw client pays as well, and the difference between the loops is a lower bound on that work, not a measurement of it.

documents.t: An instruction count holds the runtime, this crate and the AWS SDK's work on the service's thread: building and signing each request, the HTTP exchange and parsing each answer. A delivery pays its share of a ReceiveMessage and a DeleteMessage of its own, and a reply adds a SendMessage. So most of every figure is the SDK's work rather than this crate's, and the figures are not comparable with those of a broker whose client works on threads of its own. The same count costs more time where it misses the cache, so a count is not a time. Every figure is the steady state, the difference between a run of 1000 deliveries and one of 2000. Loading the AWS configuration, resolving the queue, reading its visibility timeout and the first allocations behind them are the cold start, paid once.

The stand is LocalStack, an emulator of SQS and SNS, not the hosted service. It answers over plain HTTP on the loopback, which leaves out the TLS handshake, the credential refresh and the latency of a region. The comparison stays valid, because all three loops talk to the same emulator. The throughput does not carry over: a queue in a region answers on another timescale. All three loops ask for a 20-second wait. On a queue with a backlog the wait never elapses, because a receive answers as soon as it has messages. The wait decides only what an empty queue costs. A row is one consumer reading one queue with a small body. It measures what a delivery costs inside this crate, not what SQS can carry. The FIFO row spreads its messages over 64 message groups, so a receive always finds a group that is not held. The numbers are a snapshot of one machine on one day, with the build recorded beside them. They are measured again by hand, on a machine given to the run alone: the differences they show are smaller than the noise of a shared one.

The runtime above it is the same for every broker. Everything SQS-specific is in this crate: the SqsQueue descriptor, what an outcome does to a message, and how a reply reaches a queue or a topic. The crate subscribes, takes batches and partition keys, and describes its server in the generated document. Publishing to SNS needs the sns feature. Each subscription is one queue, read by a pump task of its own. The pump long-polls the queue and keeps at most one batch ahead of the handlers. Each delivery starts a task that extends its visibility while a handler holds it. The pump and the extenders run on the runtime that connected the broker, whichever thread opened the stream. The connected broker and every publisher share one connection: the SDK clients, a closed flag, and caches of queue URLs and topic ARNs. The SDK opens an HTTP connection on the runtime of the request that needs it, and the connection makes progress only while that runtime runs. So each runtime sends through clients of its own. The broker's runtime uses the set that connect built. A handler thread with a runtime of its own builds a set on its first request, from the same configuration and credentials, and a busy thread never stalls the broker's connections. SqsPublish sends to a queue with SendMessage, and SnsPublish publishes to a topic with Publish. The publishers take the buffer the reply was encoded into, and a body SQS accepts as text becomes the request body without a copy. Any other payload travels base64-encoded with a marker attribute and is decoded on receive.

Under the testing feature, a test connects the broker in process instead. The connected broker, its subscriptions, its publishers and its deliveries then talk to an account that lives in the test. A build without the feature carries no trace of it: the compiler checks that the transport and the delivery are exactly the size of their live forms. The account answers the calls this crate makes, and refuses what SQS refuses with the error a live call reports. It models what a service's logic depends on: competing receivers, receives of up to ten, visibility and its extension, the receive count, the redrive to a dead-letter queue, FIFO groups and the five-minute deduplication window, and SNS fan-out to subscribed queues. Some things belong to the live service only. Every queue and topic the service names exists in process, and a message sent to a queue no subscription reads is dropped. A descriptor that names no visibility gets 30 seconds, the default of a new queue. A standard queue keeps its order in process, while SQS does not, so a test asserts order only on a FIFO queue. Credentials are not checked. How the pieces start and stop is on Lifecycle, and the way of one message on Path.

Without workers, one loop runs the handler for each message in turn, and nothing runs side by side. workers(n) runs up to n handlers at once, in no particular order. workers(n, by_key) runs n lanes, and a message goes to the lane its key hashes to. The key is the message's PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, which holds its FIFO message group. So a group never spreads over two lanes, and the order Groups keeps on the queue is kept in the service. Lanes fewer than groups serve several groups each. A standard queue has no groups: a message published there with the header carries it as an attribute and goes to its key's lane, and a message without it rotates over the lanes. The pump stays at most one receive ahead of the handlers. A message it received and has not handed over yet is kept invisible by its extender meanwhile. A FIFO queue also holds back a group while one of its messages is in flight, which keeps a group's next message out of the service until the previous one settles or its timeout lapses. Several replicas of a service, or several subscriptions on one queue, compete for its messages: SQS hands each message to one of them. The in-process transport keeps the order of a standard queue, which SQS does not, so a test that asserts order uses a FIFO queue. A batch handler takes one receive at a time, up to the size the mount site names and at most ten, so a batch is often smaller than that size.

Connect loads the AWS configuration through the SDK's default chain, with the endpoint and region the broker names, and sets a 25-second timeout per attempt, above the 20-second long poll. The SDK fetches credentials lazily, on the first request. In a service that request is the first subscription's GetQueueUrl, so a bad credential fails the start on subscribe. Each subscription's SqsQueue is checked first: an empty name, a wait over 20 seconds or a visibility outside one second to 12 hours is SqsError::InvalidQueue before any call to AWS, as Startup shows. Then the subscription resolves the queue URL, or creates the queue under create_if_missing. It writes the redrive policy when the registration declares max_attempts and dead_letter. It reads the queue's own visibility timeout when the descriptor names none. Then it starts the pump. A receive error reaches the subscription's stream as an item. A queue that no longer exists ends the pump, and any other error makes it wait one second before the next receive. Shutdown marks the connection closed and returns (): the SDK clients have nothing to close or flush. A publisher created before shutdown answers SqsError::NotConnected afterwards.

It stays in the queue until it is deleted or its retention ends: 4 days by default, up to 14 A producer sends one message per SendMessage call. The queue keeps it until a consumer deletes it or the retention period ends, four days by default and fourteen at most. A message is a text body of up to 1 MiB and up to ten message attributes. A consumer asks for messages with ReceiveMessage. One call returns at most ten. With long polling the call waits up to 20 seconds and answers as soon as a message is there. A received message is not removed: it stays in the queue, hidden from the other consumers, as Visibility draws. So the consumers that poll one queue share its messages. A standard queue delivers every message at least once, sometimes twice, and keeps the order only on a best-effort basis. A FIFO queue, whose name ends in .fifo, delivers the messages of one message group in order, as Groups draws. SQS bills per request, not per message. This crate always asks for ten messages per receive, even for a subscription that handles one message at a time, and hands the batch over one by one. The model is Amazon SQS's own (basic architecture, long polling, message quotas).

A FIFO queue delivers each message group in order: while a group has a message in flight, its next message waits, and the other groups go on. A FIFO queue with three message groups: the group with a message in flight waits, the other two deliverreceiveFIFO queue orders.fifoalice1in flight2waits3waitsbob1delivered2queued3queuedcarol1delivered2queuedConsumer: one ReceiveMessagegets bob 1 and carol 1, alice waitsA repeat of a MessageDeduplicationId within five minutesis accepted and not delivered The diagram as text FIFO queue orders.fifo: alice; 1 in flight; 2 waits; 3 waits; bob; 1 delivered; 2 queued; 3 queued; carol; 1 delivered; 2 queued FIFO queue orders.fifo → Consumer: one ReceiveMessage gets bob 1 and carol 1, alice waits: receive A repeat of a MessageDeduplicationId within five minutes is accepted and not delivered Every send to a FIFO queue names a MessageGroupId. The messages of one group are delivered in the order they were sent. While a message of a group is in flight, the queue hands out no other message of that group. The group moves on once that message is deleted or its visibility timeout lapses. Different groups do not wait for each other, so the groups are the unit of parallel work. Each send also carries a MessageDeduplicationId. A send that repeats an id within five minutes is accepted and not delivered. A queue with content-based deduplication derives the id from a SHA-256 hash of the body, and an id the send names takes precedence. This crate picks the group of a publish from the most specific place that names one: the call's SqsPublishOptions, then the message's PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, then the group the policy fixed, then default. It always sends a deduplication id: the one the call names, or one unique to the process. So two sends of the same body are two messages unless the service names the same id for both. A group or deduplication id set for a standard queue is refused with SqsError::NotFifo. On delivery, the group arrives in PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, and Lanes keys the workers by it. An SNS FIFO topic delivers only to FIFO queues, and the message keeps its group on the way, as Topics draws. The behaviour is Amazon SQS's own (FIFO key terms, message group id, deduplication id).

Every Publish to the topic becomes one message in each subscribed queue, so two services that read two queues both see every message. Within one queue, the consumers compete as on Queues. With raw message delivery, the queue receives the body as it was published, and the message attributes become SQS message attributes. Without it, the queue receives a JSON envelope that holds the body and the attributes. A subscription made by subscribe_queue_to_topic turns raw delivery on, so a handler on the queue reads the same body and headers the publisher sent. SNS sends to a queue only when the queue's access policy allows the SNS service sqs:SendMessage on behalf of the topic. subscribe_queue_to_topic adds a statement scoped to the topic through aws:SourceArn and keeps the statements already in the policy. A topic named by name resolves through CreateTopic, which returns the ARN of an existing topic and creates a missing one. The ARN is cached after the first publish. The parts of ruststream-sqs-sns an SQS service uses, one page per component: the broker (SqsBroker), its queue subscriptions, its publish policies for queues and SNS topics, and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on. One subscription reads one queue with long polling, and SQS settles each delivery with its own calls. A slice handler receives a whole ReceiveMessage call as one batch. A FIFO queue carries the framework's partition key as its message group. SNS is a publisher here: a topic fans a message out to the queues subscribed to it, and each queue is read the ordinary way. With the asyncapi feature, the generated document describes the queues and topics in SQS and SNS terms. Category What it covers Broker the broker, its credentials and endpoint, startup, shutdown, the prelude and the error type Subscriptions the queue a handler reads, long polling, visibility, queue creation, batches and FIFO queues Settlement what each outcome does to the message, deferred retries and dead-letter queues Delivery what a delivery carries: headers as message attributes, the receive count, the message group and the body Publishing sending to queues, FIFO message groups and deduplication ids SNS publishing to SNS topics and subscribing queues to them AsyncAPI the server, channel and topic bindings in the generated document Testing the in-process account a test runs on, and tests against a running stack

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks SQS: the server, the queue behind each channel, and the topic of a fan-out position. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds the specification's sqs binding, version 0.3.0, and with the sns feature its sns binding, version 1.0.0. A server reports where the service connects. A channel reports the queue behind it, whether the service reads it or publishes to it. A fan-out position's channel reports its topic. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the descriptors and the destinations the mount sites resolved. A setting the queue holds but the service did not name stays out, because reading it takes a connection. The document is published and shared, so no binding carries a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.8", features = ["asyncapi", "sns"] } The service registers its broker under the label sqs, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example sqs_asyncapi --features asyncapi,sns -- asyncapi gen prints the document. Each channel carries an sqs binding: the queue's name and FIFO flag, and the polling settings a subscription names. The binding holds one queue object. name is the queue's name, and fifoQueue is true for a name ending in .fifo, the suffix that makes a queue FIFO. A subscription's channel adds receiveMessageWaitTime, the long-poll wait in seconds, 20 unless the descriptor names another. It adds visibilityTimeout when the descriptor names a visibility; the queue's own timeout takes a connection to read, so the document leaves it out. A channel the service publishes to through SqsPublish reports the queue the mount site resolved. That is a reply("dest") clause, a reply type's #[outgoing(name)], or the name of a slot entry. Its binding has name and fifoQueue only: the polling belongs to the subscription that reads the queue.

The channel orders reports its queue and both polling settings, and shipments.fifo a FIFO queue polled with the default wait. The channel confirmations reports the queue the reply clause names. Macros Manual examples/sqs_asyncapi.rs #[subscriber( SqsQueue::new("orders") .wait(Duration::from_secs(10)) .visibility(Duration::from_secs(30)), reply("confirmations") )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("shipments.fifo"))] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_asyncapi.rs /// The queue `orders`, polled for up to ten seconds per receive, each message hidden for thirty /// seconds while it is handled. fn orders() -> SqsQueue { SqsQueue::new("orders") .wait(Duration::from_secs(10)) .visibility(Duration::from_secs(30)) } /// A FIFO queue: the `.fifo` suffix says so. fn shipments() -> SqsQueue { SqsQueue::new("shipments.fifo") } The binding of orders in the document: { "sqs": { "bindingVersion": "0.3.0", "queue": { "name": "orders", "fifoQueue": false, "visibilityTimeout": 30, "receiveMessageWaitTime": 10 } } }

The server reports the host clients connect to, the endpoint's or the region's, with the protocol sqs, never a credential and never a protocol version. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the host and port of the broker's endpoint; the scheme, any user info and the path stay out. A broker with no endpoint reports the regional host of its region, such as sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com, or sqs.cn-north-1.amazonaws.com.cn in the China partition. The endpoint and the region are the ones named on the broker, or else the ones of the config given to from_config. A region the SDK resolves from the environment is known only once the service connects, after the document is built, so such a broker reports sqs.amazonaws.com. The protocol is sqs. protocolVersion stays out: SQS has one wire protocol, and a client matches no version of it. SNS publishes go through the same broker, so they share its server. Credentials come from the SDK's chain or a prebuilt configuration once the service runs, and the document is built before that. No credential reaches it.

The broker reaches its region through the regional endpoint. Its server in the document is sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com with the protocol sqs. Macros Manual examples/sqs_asyncapi.rs /// The service's region, through its regional endpoint. fn broker() -> SqsBroker { SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com") .region("eu-west-1") } examples/manual/sqs_asyncapi.rs /// The service's region, through its regional endpoint. fn broker() -> SqsBroker { SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com") .region("eu-west-1") }

A fan-out position reports its topic through an sns binding, with a FIFO ordering object on a .fifo topic. A channel the service publishes to through SnsPublish carries the sns binding instead of the sqs one. name is the topic the mount site resolved, from a reply clause, a reply type's #[outgoing(name)] or a slot entry. A topic whose name ends in .fifo adds ordering, with type set to FIFO. Its contentBasedDeduplication is false: every FIFO send this crate makes carries a deduplication id of its own, which wins over one derived from the body. A standard topic carries no ordering object, which the specification reads as a standard topic.

The reply of settle fans out from the FIFO topic payment-events.fifo. SqsBroker connects a service to Amazon SQS; new only records the configuration, and the runtime builds the SDK clients at startup. SqsBroker::new takes no arguments and does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[app] builder. Left as it is, the broker takes the region, the credentials and the endpoint from the AWS SDK's default chain: the environment, the shared profile files, and the instance or container role. The credentials page shows a configuration the service builds itself, and the endpoint page a local stack. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedSqsBroker. The connect loads the AWS configuration and builds the SQS client, and the SNS client with the sns feature. Every subscription and every publisher of the service opens against that connected form, and startup resolves each subscription's queue before the service reads anything. At shutdown the runtime marks the connection closed. A request goes out through the SDK clients of the runtime that sends it. A handler on a dedicated thread, set with threads(n), gets clients of its own on its first request, built from the same configuration and sharing its credentials. Its connections stay in its own pool, so the broker's requests never wait on a thread that is busy computing. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the queue orders with the default settings. SqsQueue carries the settings of one subscription, such as the long-polling wait and the visibility timeout.

The handler reads the queue orders, each receive waiting up to 20 seconds for a message. Macros Manual examples/sqs_service.rs /// Reads the queue `orders`, each receive waiting up to 20 seconds for a message. /// /// A fresh local stack has no queues, so the descriptor creates the queue at startup. A /// production service drops that step and takes the queue from its infrastructure. #[subscriber( SqsQueue::new("orders") .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)) .create_if_missing() )] async fn handle(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order received"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_service.rs /// Logs each order it receives. struct Receive; impl Handle<Order> for Receive { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order received"); ready(Ok(())) } } The app mounts it on a broker that reads its configuration from the environment. With AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566, AWS_REGION and test keys set, cargo run --example sqs_service --features testing -- run starts it against a local stack. Macros Manual examples/sqs_service.rs #[app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(SqsBroker::new(), |b| b.include(handle)) } examples/manual/sqs_service.rs /// Reads the queue `orders`, each receive waiting up to 20 seconds for a message. A fresh local /// stack has no queues, so the subscription creates the queue at startup. fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqsBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), Receive) .build() .name("orders") .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)) .create_if_missing(), ) }) }

The AWS SDK's default chain supplies the region and the credentials, fetched on the first request; from_config takes a prebuilt SdkConfig instead. A broker built with new loads its configuration with aws_config when it connects. The region comes from AWS_REGION or the shared profile, and the credentials from the environment, the shared profile files, SSO, or the instance or container role. The SDK fetches the credentials on the first request, a subscription's GetQueueUrl at startup, so a service with a subscription meets a missing credential there. The configuration follows the SDK's latest behaviour version. The connect also sets a per-attempt timeout of 25 seconds, above the 20 seconds a long poll waits. from_config takes an aws_config::SdkConfig the service builds itself: a named profile, a pinned behaviour version, its own HTTP client or credential provider. The credentials, the timeouts and the rest of the SDK's settings come from that config. An endpoint or a region named on the broker replaces the config's own, and what the broker does not name stays as the config has it. test_credentials belongs to new: a prebuilt config signs with its own credential provider. The SDK sets no attempt timeout of its own, so a config without one lets every long poll run its full wait. A config with an attempt timeout under 20 seconds ends every long poll early, and each receive fails; the example sets 25 seconds, as new does. Transport security is the SDK's HTTPS client in both cases. The service's role needs these permissions: Action When sqs:GetQueueUrl, sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility every subscription sqs:GetQueueAttributes a subscription that names no visibility, and the dead-letter queue of a redrive policy sqs:SetQueueAttributes a subscription with a redrive policy, and the queue of subscribe_queue_to_topic sqs:CreateQueue a subscription with create_if_missing sqs:SendMessage every publish to a queue sns:Publish every publish to a topic, and sns:CreateTopic for a topic named by name rather than ARN sns:Subscribe subscribe_queue_to_topic, with sns:CreateTopic on the topic and sqs:GetQueueUrl, sqs:GetQueueAttributes and sqs:SetQueueAttributes on the queue

endpoint, region and test_credentials point the broker at a local stack; queue URLs the service returns are rebased onto the endpoint. endpoint replaces the AWS endpoint with an address such as http://localhost:4566, where LocalStack listens. region sets the region every request is signed for. test_credentials signs requests with a fixed dummy key: a local stack checks that a request is signed and ignores the key. Each step overrides only its own setting, and the SDK's default chain resolves the rest. On a broker built with from_config, endpoint and region replace the config's own, and the config supplies the rest. A local stack returns queue URLs on a host of its own choosing, which may not resolve from the service. The broker keeps the path of each URL and puts the configured endpoint in front of it, so a stack's host strategy changes nothing. An endpoint from AWS_ENDPOINT_URL or from the config given to from_config is rebased the same way. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the endpoint's host and port as the server. A broker with no endpoint and a known region is reported by the regional host, such as sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com.

The service runs against LocalStack on port 4566. Macros Manual examples/sqs_broker_endpoint.rs /// The broker for a local stack at `endpoint`, such as `LocalStack` on port 4566. The stack checks /// that a request is signed and ignores the key, so test credentials are enough. fn broker(endpoint: &str) -> SqsBroker { SqsBroker::new() .endpoint(endpoint) .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials() } #[app] fn app() -> impl App { service(broker("http://localhost:4566"), "orders".to_owned()) } examples/manual/sqs_broker_endpoint.rs /// The broker for a local stack at `endpoint`, such as `LocalStack` on port 4566. The stack checks /// that a request is signed and ignores the key, so test credentials are enough. fn broker(endpoint: &str) -> SqsBroker { SqsBroker::new() .endpoint(endpoint) .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials() } fn app() -> impl App { service(broker("http://localhost:4566"), "orders".to_owned()) }

SqsError is the crate's one error type: configuration, queues, receives, publishes, SNS admin, queue access policies, a closed connection and refused settings. Each variant names the step that failed and the queue or topic it was about. The SDK's failure behind it is its source, formatted with its whole cause chain, so the SDK's error types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Config the in-process mode was asked of a broker whose handles already connected to AWS Queue a queue could not be resolved, created, read or given its redrive policy Receive a receive from an open subscription failed Publish SQS refused a message, or SNS refused a notification Admin a topic could not be created or a queue subscribed to it (sns feature) QueuePolicy a queue's access policy could not be read or written while subscribe_queue_to_topic granted a topic the right to send to it (sns feature) NotConnected a publisher was used before the broker connected, or after it shut down InvalidQueue a descriptor is out of range: an empty name, a wait or a visibility SQS does not allow IncompleteRedrive a registration declared max_attempts without dead_letter, or the other way round (dead letters) NotFifo a publish named a group id or a deduplication id for a standard queue or topic A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it in the cause chain of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it as the source of the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. A publish refused before its request was built (a closed connection, a queue that does not resolve, a header or a FIFO setting SQS does not take) hands the unsent message back with the error; one that SQS or SNS refused comes back without it, because the client consumed the body. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

A shipment to a warehouse queue that is not FIFO is refused with NotFifo. A retry would be refused again, so the handler drops the order and logs the error; any other failure is retried. Macros Manual examples/sqs_broker_errors.rs /// Whether SQS refused a publish because its destination is not a FIFO queue. The `SqsError` is /// the source of the publish error, or a source further down its chain. fn not_fifo(err: &(dyn Error + 'static)) -> bool { let mut cause = Some(err); while let Some(err) = cause { if let Some(SqsError::NotFifo { .. }) = err.downcast_ref::<SqsError>() { return true; } cause = err.source(); } false } /// Ships an order through its warehouse's FIFO queue, in the customer's message group. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders"))] async fn ship( order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = shipments .message(&shipment) .to(order.warehouse.as_str()) .group_id(&order.customer) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // A standard queue has no message groups, and a retry would be refused again. Err(err) if not_fifo(&err) => { tracing::error!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "not a FIFO queue"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not sent"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/sqs_broker_errors.rs /// Whether SQS refused a publish because its destination is not a FIFO queue. The `SqsError` is /// the source of the publish error, or a source further down its chain. fn not_fifo(err: &(dyn Error + 'static)) -> bool { let mut cause = Some(err); while let Some(err) = cause { if let Some(SqsError::NotFifo { .. }) = err.downcast_ref::<SqsError>() { return true; } cause = err.source(); } false } /// Ships an order through its warehouse's FIFO queue, in the customer's message group. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = outs .get(Shipments) .message(&shipment) .to(order.warehouse.as_str()) .group_id(&order.customer) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // A standard queue has no message groups, and a retry would be refused again. Err(err) if not_fifo(&err) => { tracing::error!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "not a FIFO queue"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not sent"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } } }

One glob, ruststream_sqs_sns::prelude, brings the core prelude, the broker, the queue descriptor, the policies and the publish steps. use ruststream_sqs_sns::prelude::*; is the one import a routes file writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], #[app], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds SqsBroker, the descriptor SqsQueue with its mount-site steps SqsSubscription, the publish steps SqsPublishSteps with SqsPublishOptions, and the publishers SqsPublisher and, with sns, SnsPublisher. The queue policy comes under the name every broker crate gives it: Publish is SqsPublish, so a mount site reads the same on every broker. SnsPublish, with the sns feature, keeps its own name. Two broker preludes in one file collide on Publish; the prefixed types at the crate root tell them apart. The constants RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER and PARTITION_KEY_HEADER and the error type SqsError are imported from the crate root. A handler file globs the core prelude and names no broker type: an injected publisher is bounded Out<impl Publisher, Marker>. The one exception is a body that sets a per-message setting: group_id or deduplication_id needs SqsPublishSteps in scope and the slot bounded Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Marker>, both from this prelude.

The descriptor, the broker and the reply policy all come from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/sqs_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_sqs_sns::prelude::*; #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders").wait(Duration::from_secs(20)), reply)] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> OrderAccepted { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); OrderAccepted { id: order.id } } #[app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqsBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(accept).out_reply(Publish::default()) }) } examples/manual/sqs_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_sqs_sns::prelude::*; struct Accept; impl Handle<Order, OrderAccepted> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderAccepted, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); ready(Ok(OrderAccepted { id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqsBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), Accept) .reply() .build() .name("orders") .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)), ) .out_reply(Publish::default()) }) }

Shutdown marks the connection closed; a publisher handed out earlier reports SqsError::NotConnected instead of sending. SQS calls complete one by one, and the SDK clients hold nothing to flush. The runtime stops the subscriptions and marks the connection closed, which is the whole teardown. A delivery a handler had not settled returns to its queue when its visibility timeout lapses. A publisher taken with SqsBroker::publisher shares the broker's connection. It can be taken before the app starts and handed to code outside the handlers, such as an HTTP endpoint. It sends once the runtime has connected the broker. After shutdown it returns SqsError::NotConnected inside the core's PublishError, and never sends over a connection the service has given up. A publisher of a lifecycle hook or an Out slot behaves the same way.

The service hands a publisher to code outside its handlers. Macros Manual examples/sqs_broker_shutdown.rs /// The service, and a publisher for code outside its handlers, such as an HTTP endpoint that /// takes orders. The publisher shares the broker's connection, from startup to shutdown. fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> (impl App<State = ()>, SqsPublisher) { let intake = broker.publisher(); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(handle.name(queue).create_if_missing()) }); (app, intake) } examples/manual/sqs_broker_shutdown.rs /// The service, and a publisher for code outside its handlers, such as an HTTP endpoint that /// takes orders. The publisher shares the broker's connection, from startup to shutdown. fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> (impl App<State = ()>, SqsPublisher) { let intake = broker.publisher(); let app = RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), Receive) .build() .name(queue) .create_if_missing(), ) }); (app, intake) }

Startup opens every subscription: it resolves the queue URL, reads the queue's visibility timeout and writes a declared redrive policy. Each subscription first checks its descriptor, before any call to AWS. An empty queue name, a wait above 20 seconds or a visibility outside one second to twelve hours fails startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue. The subscription then resolves the queue name to its URL with GetQueueUrl, once, and the broker caches the answer. A queue URL in the descriptor is used as it is. A queue that does not exist fails startup with SqsError::Queue, naming the queue, unless the subscription creates it. A registration with a redrive policy writes the policy onto the queue next. A subscription that names no visibility reads the queue's own timeout with GetQueueAttributes, and holds every delivery under it. Every request runs under the per-attempt timeout of 25 seconds that new sets on connect. A broker built from a config runs under the timeouts that config carries. The first request also fetches the credentials, so a missing credential or an unreachable endpoint fails startup too. The in-process account a TestApp test runs on has every queue the service names, so a missing queue shows only against a running stack. A descriptor out of range fails TestApp::start as it fails a real startup.

The subscription reads a queue the infrastructure created, and takes its visibility timeout from the queue. Macros Manual examples/sqs_broker_startup.rs #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn handle(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order received"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Reads `queue`, which the infrastructure creates. The subscription names no visibility /// timeout, so startup reads the queue's own. fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(handle.name(queue).wait(Duration::from_secs(20))) }) } examples/manual/sqs_broker_startup.rs struct Receive; impl Handle<Order> for Receive { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order received"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Reads `queue`, which the infrastructure creates. The subscription names no visibility /// timeout, so startup reads the queue's own. fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), Receive) .build() .name(queue) .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)), ) }) }

A delivery carries its payload and its headers; each header is one SQS message attribute, String or Binary, at most ten. A header the service takes as text travels as a String attribute, and any other value as a Binary one. A handler reads the same bytes either way, and never sees which type carried them. No envelope wraps the message, so any other SQS producer or consumer reads it as it is. SQS and SNS take at most ten attributes on one message. A publish that needs more fails before it is sent, with SqsError::TooManyAttributes: it names the destination, the count, the limit, the attributes, and the one the crate added, if it added one. An attribute name is 1 to 256 letters, digits, _, - and ., and a value is never empty. A message SQS refuses fails the publish with SqsError::Publish, and the in-process account refuses it the same way. A message is at most 1 MiB, body and attributes together. A handler reads the headers as a typed contract with Headers<T>, or one by one through cx.headers(). Two headers have meanings of their own: RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER carries the queue's receive count, and PARTITION_KEY_HEADER the FIFO message group. A payload SQS would not take as text travels base64-encoded with one more attribute, as the body page describes. The crate adds no per-delivery context field, so a handler takes no Ctx<K> parameter here; what a delivery carries beyond its payload is in its headers.

An order carries its tenant and a trace id as two message attributes, and the handler reads them as one contract. Macros Manual examples/sqs_delivery_headers.rs /// The headers an order carries: two message attributes on the queue. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize)] struct OrderMeta { tenant: String, trace: Option<String>, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders"))] async fn bill(order: &Order, Headers(meta): Headers<OrderMeta>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, meta.tenant, trace = ?meta.trace, "order billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_delivery_headers.rs /// The headers an order carries: two message attributes on the queue. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct OrderMeta { tenant: String, trace: Option<String>, } struct Bill; impl Handle<Message<OrderMeta, Order>> for Bill { fn handle( &self, msg: &Message<OrderMeta, Order>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let (order, meta) = (&msg.body, &msg.headers); tracing::info!(order.id, meta.tenant, trace = ?meta.trace, "order billed"); ready(Ok(())) } }

SQS bodies are text, so a payload SQS would refuse travels base64 with a marker attribute and is decoded again on receive. SQS takes a narrower set of characters than UTF-8 in a body. It refuses the control characters other than tab, line feed and carriage return, and the two non-characters at the end of the basic plane. A payload that is such text, a JSON document for one, travels as it is. Any other payload travels base64-encoded, with the attribute ruststream-payload-encoding set to base64: bytes that are not UTF-8, and equally valid UTF-8 with control characters, which a binary codec often emits. The receiving side decodes the body again before the handler sees it. A handler receives the bytes the producer published, and the marker attribute never reaches its headers. An attribute of that name with any other value is not the marker, and it arrives as a header. The marker counts towards the ten attributes of a message, so a binary payload leaves nine for the service's own headers. A publish with a header named ruststream-payload-encoding fails with SqsError::InvalidHeader, because the receiving side would take it for the marker. SQS refuses an empty body, and so does the in-process account. A handler that reads the bytes itself takes a #[derive(Deserialized)] newtype over &[u8], and no codec runs. The type borrows the delivery's buffer, so nothing is copied.

The handler stores thumbnails, raw image bytes that SQS would not take as text. Macros Manual examples/sqs_delivery_body.rs /// A thumbnail as the producer sent it: raw image bytes, read without a codec. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Thumbnail<'a>(&'a [u8]); #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn store(thumbnail: &Thumbnail<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(bytes = thumbnail.0.len(), "thumbnail stored"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_delivery_body.rs /// A thumbnail as the producer sent it: raw image bytes, read without a codec. struct Thumbnail<'a>(&'a [u8]); impl Deserialized for Thumbnail<'_> { type Output<'a> = Thumbnail<'a>; type Error = Infallible; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Thumbnail<'_>, Self::Error> { Ok(Thumbnail(payload)) } } // Routes the type onto the lane of payloads that read themselves. impl Input for Thumbnail<'_> { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Thumbnail<'static>>; } struct Store; // For every lifetime of the payload it borrows. impl<'p> Handle<Thumbnail<'p>> for Store { fn handle( &self, thumbnail: &Thumbnail<'p>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(bytes = thumbnail.0.len(), "thumbnail stored"); ready(Ok(())) } }

PARTITION_KEY_HEADER is the portable spelling of the FIFO message group: sent as MessageGroupId on a FIFO queue, as an ordinary attribute on a standard one, and read back on delivery either way. The header's name is partition-key, the one the core's in-memory broker uses, so a service that sets it runs unchanged on another broker. A publish to a .fifo queue or topic sends it as the message group, not as an attribute, and a delivery from a FIFO queue carries the group back in it. A standard queue or topic has no message groups, so there the header travels as an ordinary String attribute and counts toward the ten a message carries; a delivery carries it back as the same header. The group of a FIFO publish resolves from the most specific setting: the call's own group_id step, then this header, then the group the publish policy fixed. A FIFO publish that names none goes under the group default. SQS hands out one group's messages in order, and holds the group back while one of its messages is in flight, as the FIFO page describes.

The router forwards each order to the packing line in the customer's group, and the packer reads the group back. Macros Manual examples/sqs_delivery_partition_key.rs /// Forwards each order to the packing line in the customer's message group, so one customer's /// orders are packed in the order they were placed. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders"))] async fn route(order: &Order, Out(packing): Out<impl Publisher, Packing>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, order.customer.clone()); match packing .message(order) .to("packing.fifo") .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } /// Reads the group back from the delivery. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("packing.fifo"))] async fn pack(order: &Order, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let group = cx .headers() .get(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .map(String::from_utf8_lossy); tracing::info!(order.id, ?group, "order packed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_delivery_partition_key.rs /// Forwards each order to the packing line in the customer's message group, so one customer's /// orders are packed in the order they were placed. struct Route; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Route where Entry: OutEntry<Packing, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, order.customer.clone()); let sent = outs .get(Packing) .message(order) .to("packing.fifo") .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } /// Reads the group back from the delivery. struct Pack; impl Handle<Order> for Pack { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let group = ctx .headers() .get(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .map(String::from_utf8_lossy); tracing::info!(order.id, ?group, "order packed"); ready(Ok(())) } }

RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER carries the queue's ApproximateReceiveCount, one on the first delivery, so a handler can tell the last attempt. The header's name is sqs-receive-count, and its value is the count as decimal text. SQS counts every receive of a message, the one in hand included. A retry or a deferred retry returns the message to the same queue, so the count goes on rising. A redrive policy caps the same count. After max_attempts receives, SQS moves the message to the dead-letter queue on the receive that follows. A handler that compares the header with the cap knows when it holds the last attempt. SQS calls the count approximate: on a standard queue a message is delivered at least once, and a duplicate receive counts too.

A declined payment is tried three times. On the third receive the handler sends it to review and acknowledges it, so it never reaches the dead-letter queue. Macros Manual examples/sqs_delivery_receive_count.rs /// How many times the queue hands a payment over before it moves it to the dead-letter queue. const ATTEMPTS: u32 = 3; #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn charge( payment: &Payment, cx: &mut Context<'_>, Out(review): Out<impl Publisher, Review>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.card_accepted { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let receives: u32 = cx .headers() .get(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| str::from_utf8(count).ok()?.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if receives < ATTEMPTS { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } // The last attempt: a person looks at the payment before the queue gives up on it. tracing::warn!(payment.id, receives, "payment declined, sent to review"); match review .message(payment) .to("payments-review") .publish() .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } #[app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqsBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(ATTEMPTS)) .dead_letter("payments-dead") .out(Review, Publish::default()) .build() }) } examples/manual/sqs_delivery_receive_count.rs /// How many times the queue hands a payment over before it moves it to the dead-letter queue. const ATTEMPTS: u32 = 3; struct Charge; impl<Entry> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Charge where Entry: OutEntry<Review, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if payment.card_accepted { return Ok(()); } let receives: u32 = ctx .headers() .get(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| str::from_utf8(count).ok()?.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if receives < ATTEMPTS { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } // The last attempt: a person looks at the payment before the queue gives up on it. tracing::warn!(payment.id, receives, "payment declined, sent to review"); let sent = outs .get(Review) .message(payment) .to("payments-review") .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqsBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), Charge) .build() .name("payments"), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(ATTEMPTS)) .dead_letter("payments-dead") .out(Review, Publish::default()) .build() }) }

SqsPublish, Publish in the prelude, sends each message to the queue it names; it is the broker's default, so a reply needs no policy. A mount site names it wherever a registration publishes: .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply. A lifecycle hook takes it too, b.after_startup(Publish::default(), ..), and is handed the live publisher. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup into an SqsPublisher. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through this one, so .out_reply(Publish::default()) only restates the default. The destination is a queue name or a queue URL. A name resolves to its URL through GetQueueUrl, and the broker caches the answer. A publish never creates a queue: a name the account lacks fails the publish with an error. A publish returns once SQS has accepted the message, or with the error SQS reported. The payload is the message body, and the headers travel as message attributes. SQS takes a message of up to 1 MiB, body and attributes together. On a .fifo queue every send carries a message group and a deduplication id. A handler sets either for one message through SqsPublishOptions. SnsPublish sends the same messages to an SNS topic instead.

The confirmation names its queue, and the mount site binds no policy for the reply. deduplication_id names one message's idempotency key on a FIFO destination; left unnamed, every send gets a process-unique id. A FIFO queue accepts a message whose deduplication id it has seen in the last five minutes and does not deliver it again. The repeated publish succeeds, so the sender cannot tell the two apart and does not need to. An id derived from the input makes a handler's publish idempotent: SQS delivers a message at least once, and a second run of the handler sends the same id. The id is a step of one publish, never a setting of the policy. A constant id would collapse everything a position sends into one message. A send that names none carries an id this crate makes unique within the process, rs-<pid>-<sequence>. Two identical payloads sent on purpose therefore stay two messages, even on a queue with content-based deduplication. The step on a standard queue fails the publish with SqsError::NotFifo. A FIFO topic takes the same step through SnsPublish.

A payment SQS delivers twice leads to one charge: both runs send the charge under the payment's id. Macros Manual examples/sqs_publishing_deduplication.rs /// SQS delivers a message at least once, so this handler may run twice for one payment. Both /// runs send the charge under the payment's id, and the FIFO queue keeps the first. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn bill( payment: &Payment, Out(charges): Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Charges>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let charge = Charge { payment_id: payment.id, amount: payment.amount, }; let sent = charges .message(&charge) .group_id(&payment.account) .deduplication_id(format!("payment-{}", payment.id)) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge not sent"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_publishing_deduplication.rs /// SQS delivers a message at least once, so this handler may run twice for one payment. Both /// runs send the charge under the payment's id, and the FIFO queue keeps the first. struct Bill; impl<Entry> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Bill where Entry: OutEntry<Charges, Wire: Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let charge = Charge { payment_id: payment.id, amount: payment.amount, }; let sent = outs .get(Charges) .message(&charge) .group_id(&payment.account) .deduplication_id(format!("payment-{}", payment.id)) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge not sent"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

group_id on the policy orders everything a position publishes within one group; a call's own step and the partition key win over it. A FIFO queue delivers the messages of one group in the order they were sent, one group member at a time. Messages of different groups do not wait for each other. A group belongs to a position: a slot, a reply or a lifecycle hook. Every send from that position to a .fifo destination falls back to the group its policy fixed. Three answers can be in play at once, and the most specific wins. The call's own group_id step comes first. The message's PARTITION_KEY_HEADER comes next, the spelling that travels unchanged to every other broker. The policy's group comes last, and a send that names none at all goes under "default". A FIFO delivery carries its group in the partition-key header, which is where a handler and a test read it. A group on a position that publishes to a standard queue fails the publish with SqsError::NotFifo. A partition key alone is a portable hint: it names no group on a standard queue and travels there as an ordinary attribute. SnsPublish::group_id does the same for a FIFO topic.

At startup the service replays the orders a previous run did not hand on, all in the group replay, so fulfillment receives them in the order they were taken. The place handler names each customer's group for its own messages, which wins over its slot's policy. Macros Manual examples/sqs_fifo_group.rs fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The replay keeps its own order: every message the hook sends is in the group `replay`. b.after_startup( Publish::default().group_id("replay"), async move |sqs| -> io::Result<()> { for order in pending() { sqs.message(&order) .publish() .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) }, ) .include(place) .out(Placements, Publish::default()) .build() .include(fulfil) }) } examples/manual/sqs_fifo_group.rs fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b // The replay keeps its own order: every message the hook sends is in the group `replay`. .after_startup( Publish::default().group_id("replay"), async move |sqs| -> io::Result<()> { for order in pending() { sqs.message(&order) .publish() .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) }, ) .include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()) .out(Placements, Publish::default()) .build() .include(subscriber("fulfillment.fifo", Fulfil).build()) }) }

A handler sets one message's group or deduplication id through the publish steps, bounding its slot on SqsPublishOptions. SqsPublishOptions holds the two settings one publish may differ from the next in: a message group and a deduplication id. A call site writes them through the steps of SqsPublishSteps, .group_id(..) and .deduplication_id(..) on the publish builder. A step wins over the group the policy fixed, for that one message. Both are FIFO settings: a .fifo destination takes them, and a standard one fails the publish. A handler bounds its slot as Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Marker>, which puts the steps in reach. The body imports ruststream_sqs_sns::prelude::*, the one handler file that globs this crate's prelude instead of the framework's. The same steps are on every publish surface of this crate: an injected slot, the publisher a lifecycle hook is handed, a fan-out publisher. A slot moved from SqsPublish to SnsPublish keeps the body that names them. A reply has no call site, so its policy is its whole answer. A test reads back what a publish asked for: tb.out::<Marker>().with_options(&SqsPublishOptions::default().group_id(..)).

Each customer's orders reach fulfillment in the order they were placed: the group of each message is the customer. Macros Manual examples/sqs_fifo_group.rs /// One customer's orders reach fulfillment in the order they were placed; different customers' /// orders do not wait for each other. The group is the customer. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders"))] async fn place( order: &Order, Out(placements): Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Placements>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let placed = OrderPlaced { id: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let sent = placements .message(&placed) .group_id(&order.customer) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "order not placed"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_fifo_group.rs /// One customer's orders reach fulfillment in the order they were placed; different customers' /// orders do not wait for each other. The group is the customer. struct Place; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Place where Entry: OutEntry<Placements, Wire: Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let placed = OrderPlaced { id: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; let sent = outs .get(Placements) .message(&placed) .group_id(&order.customer) .publish() .await; if let Err(err) = sent { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "order not placed"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

Each outcome is one SQS call: ack and drop delete the message, retry makes it visible again at once. ack deletes the message with DeleteMessage. drop deletes it too, because SQS has no call that rejects a message without deleting it. retry sets the message's visibility timeout to zero, so the next receive hands it out again. retry_after sets the timeout to a delay instead. A redelivered message is the same message: the queue counts its receives, and the handler reads the count in RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER. A delivery the service never settles, as when its process stops, makes no call, and the message comes back once its visibility timeout lapses. A redrive policy caps the receives, and the queue moves a spent message to a dead-letter queue itself. In the manual form Ok(()) acknowledges the delivery and Err(outcome) settles it with that outcome.

A malformed payment is dropped, a payment the gateway was too busy for comes back at once, and a charged one is deleted. Macros Manual examples/sqs_settlement_outcomes.rs /// One payment per delivery. A malformed payment is dropped, a busy gateway gets the payment /// again at once, and a charged payment is acknowledged. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "malformed payment dropped"); // DeleteMessage: the payment never comes back. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } let attempt = cx.headers().get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); if charge_card(payment, attempt).await.is_err() { tracing::warn!(payment.id, attempt, "gateway busy"); // ChangeMessageVisibility to zero: the next receive hands it out again. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } // DeleteMessage. HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_settlement_outcomes.rs /// One payment per delivery. A malformed payment is dropped, a busy gateway gets the payment /// again at once, and a charged payment is acknowledged. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "malformed payment dropped"); // DeleteMessage: the payment never comes back. return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let attempt = ctx.headers().get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); if charge_card(payment, attempt).await.is_err() { tracing::warn!(payment.id, attempt, "gateway busy"); // ChangeMessageVisibility to zero: the next receive hands it out again. return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } // DeleteMessage. Ok(()) } }

max_attempts and dead_letter together become the queue's redrive policy, and SQS moves a spent message to the dead-letter queue itself. The cap is the policy's maxReceiveCount, at most 1000, and the destination is the queue it points at. The subscription writes the policy onto its queue with SetQueueAttributes when it opens. SQS then counts the receives and carries the message away on the receive past the cap, so nothing leaves the service. A bare queue name takes the declaration the same way as an SqsQueue. Both halves are needed: a cap without a destination, or a destination without a cap, stops the service at startup with SqsError::IncompleteRedrive, which names the missing half. The dead-letter queue has to exist at startup, unless the subscription creates its queues. A FIFO queue takes a FIFO dead-letter queue, and a standard queue a standard one. A drop normally deletes the message, but on the delivery that has spent the policy it returns the message instead, because the next receive is what moves it to the dead-letter queue. The dead-letter queue is an ordinary queue, read by an ordinary subscription. The policy needs the permissions sqs:SetQueueAttributes on the queue and sqs:GetQueueAttributes on the dead-letter queue.

An invoice that is never ready is received three times and then moves to invoices-dead, where a person takes it over. Macros Manual examples/sqs_dead_letter.rs /// A handler that is never ready. Every delivery asks to come back later, so what ends the /// message is the cap: the queue hands it over three times and then moves it. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("invoices").create_if_missing())] async fn settle(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice is not ready yet"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } /// The dead-letter queue is an ordinary queue, read by an ordinary subscription. #[subscriber("invoices-dead")] async fn escalate(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(invoice.id, "invoice escalated to a person"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_dead_letter.rs /// A handler that is never ready. Every delivery asks to come back later, so what ends the /// message is the cap: the queue hands it over three times and then moves it. struct Settle; impl Handle<Invoice> for Settle { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice is not ready yet"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))) } } /// The dead-letter queue is an ordinary queue, read by an ordinary subscription. struct Escalate; impl Handle<Invoice> for Escalate { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!(invoice.id, "invoice escalated to a person"); ready(Ok(())) } }

The cap and the dead-letter queue, written at the mount site. Macros Manual examples/sqs_dead_letter.rs fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoices", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The two steps are the queue's redrive policy: `maxReceiveCount` and the // dead-letter queue it points at. The subscription writes them when it opens. b.include(settle) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("invoices-dead") .include(escalate) }) } examples/manual/sqs_dead_letter.rs fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoices", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The two steps are the queue's redrive policy: `maxReceiveCount` and the // dead-letter queue it points at. The subscription writes them when it opens. b.include( subscriber("invoices", Settle) .build() .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("invoices").create_if_missing()), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("invoices-dead") .include(subscriber("invoices-dead", Escalate).build()) }) }

retry_after(delay) sets the message's visibility to the delay, so it returns on the same queue with its receive count, within 12 hours of its receive. SQS holds a message back natively: ChangeMessageVisibility hides it for the delay, and the next receive after that hands it out again. Nothing is republished and no copy is made, so the message keeps its id, its attributes and its receive count. SQS counts whole seconds, so a fraction of a second rounds up. SQS keeps a message hidden for at most twelve hours from its receive, so the longest delay is what remains of those twelve hours. A longer delay is shortened to end with them, and the crate logs a warning that names the queue. The delay waits on the queue, not in the service, so a service that stops in the meantime loses nothing. SQS moves the message itself, so the registration names no retry publisher, and .out_retry(..) does not compile on an SqsQueue. A redrive policy counts a deferred receive like any other. In a test, tb.advance(delay) lets the delay pass on a paused clock.

An invoice whose payment has not cleared comes back five seconds later and is settled then. Macros Manual examples/sqs_settlement_retry_after.rs /// How long an invoice whose payment has not cleared waits before it is checked again. const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(5); /// The payment of an invoice clears within seconds, so the first receive asks for the invoice /// again later and the second one settles it. #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn settle(invoice: &Invoice, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if cx.headers().get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) == Some("1") { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "payment not cleared yet"); // ChangeMessageVisibility to five seconds: nothing is republished. return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_settlement_retry_after.rs /// How long an invoice whose payment has not cleared waits before it is checked again. const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(5); /// The payment of an invoice clears within seconds, so the first receive asks for the invoice /// again later and the second one settles it. struct Settle; impl Handle<Invoice> for Settle { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) == Some("1") { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "payment not cleared yet"); // ChangeMessageVisibility to five seconds: nothing is republished. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice settled"); ready(Ok(())) } }

SnsPublish fans a reply out from an SNS topic to every queue subscribed to it; one out_reply step switches a position to it. The policy needs the crate's sns feature. A mount site names it where a registration publishes: .out_reply(SnsPublish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, SnsPublish::default()) for a slot. The destination reads the same as on SqsPublish: the reply type or the mount site names it, and the policy decides whether the name is a queue or a topic. Without the step the same reply lands on a queue of that name. The runtime pairs the policy with the connected broker into an SnsPublisher. The destination is a topic name or a topic ARN. A name resolves to its ARN through CreateTopic, which returns an existing topic as it is and creates a missing one. A name ending in .fifo is a FIFO topic, and it takes the same group and deduplication steps as a FIFO queue. A topic and a queue may share a name: each publish goes where its policy sends it. The payload is the notification's message, and the headers travel as message attributes. SNS takes a message of up to 256 KiB. SNS is a publish target only: the service reads the queues subscribed to the topic. A queue joins a topic through subscribe_queue_to_topic, or through the operator's own provisioning. Either way, SNS delivers to the queue only when the queue's access policy lets the topic send to it, and subscribe_queue_to_topic adds that statement itself.

The dependency line: ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.8", features = ["sns"] } The notification names its topic, so the handler answers with a bare reply clause. It names the topic, so the handler answers with a bare /// `reply` clause. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders-events")] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders").create_if_missing(), reply)] async fn accept(order: &PlaceOrder) -> OrderPlaced { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); OrderPlaced { id: order.id } } examples/manual/sns_fanout.rs /// The notification the topic fans out. It names the topic, so the reply takes no destination /// at the mount site. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "orders-events")] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, } struct Accept; impl Handle<PlaceOrder, OrderPlaced> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &PlaceOrder, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderPlaced, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); ready(Ok(OrderPlaced { id: order.id })) } } The mount site binds the reply position to SnsPublish, and billing and shipping each receive the order. fans_out_to names the queues an operator subscribed to a topic, so a test sees every queue the topic delivers to. A queue the service subscribes itself, through subscribe_queue_to_topic, is known to the broker. A queue an operator subscribed in AWS is known only to AWS. The step names those queues on the policy, and they apply to every topic the position publishes to. In process the account subscribes them to the topic before the publish, as the operator did. A live test waits for the subscription of each named queue to handle its copy. A queue SNS refuses, such as a FIFO queue on a standard topic, fails the publish. The step exists with the crate's testing feature, which a service enables in its [dev-dependencies]. The service builds the policy with the step under #[cfg(test)], which holds in the build of the tests beside its code. A production build neither has the step nor calls it. A test under tests/ builds the service without cfg(test). There the service gates the step on a feature of its own that enables ruststream-sqs-sns/testing, and the tests run with that feature.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.8", features = ["sns", "testing"] } The operator subscribed billing to orders-events, and the test build of the policy says so.
