subscribe_queue_to_topic subscribes a queue to a topic with raw message delivery, so payloads and headers arrive as plain SQS messages. The call takes a topic, by name or ARN, and a queue, by name or URL. A topic name resolves through CreateTopic, so a missing topic comes into being; the queue has to exist. With raw message delivery the notification's message is the queue message's body, and its attributes are the queue message's attributes. A handler on the queue therefore decodes the same payload and reads the same headers a publish to the queue would give it. SNS delivers to a queue only when the queue's access policy lets the topic send to it. Before it subscribes, the call adds that statement to the queue's policy: sqs:SendMessage for the SNS service, limited to this topic through aws:SourceArn. The statements already in the policy stay as they are. A policy that already grants the topic is not written again, so the call is safe on every start. SQS has no conditional write of a policy, so two services that grant different topics on one queue at the same moment can lose one of the grants. A policy that cannot be read or written fails the call with SqsError::QueuePolicy. The call needs sns:CreateTopic and sns:Subscribe on the topic, and sqs:GetQueueUrl, sqs:GetQueueAttributes and sqs:SetQueueAttributes on the queue (permissions). The method belongs to the connected broker, ConnectedSqsBroker. A service reaches it from an after_startup hook: it clones the app's broker before the app takes it, and the hook connects the clone. A clone connects through the connection the app's broker already holds, so in a test the call reaches the in-process account. By the time the hook runs, the subscriptions have opened their queues, create_if_missing ones included. SNS refuses a FIFO queue on a standard topic, and the call fails with SqsError::Admin. In production the topic and its subscriptions are often infrastructure that an operator provisions. A test of such a service names those queues on the policy with fans_out_to.

The hook subscribes both queues to the topic the reply fans out from. Macros Manual examples/sns_fanout.rs /// Subscribes both queues to the topic. The subscriptions have opened the queues by the time a /// startup hook runs. async fn wire_topology(broker: SqsBroker) -> io::Result<()> { let connected = broker.connect().await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; for queue in ["billing", "shipping"] { connected .subscribe_queue_to_topic("orders-events", queue) .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) } examples/manual/sns_fanout.rs /// Subscribes both queues to the topic. The subscriptions have opened the queues by the time a /// startup hook runs. async fn wire_topology(broker: SqsBroker) -> io::Result<()> { let connected = broker.connect().await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; for queue in ["billing", "shipping"] { connected .subscribe_queue_to_topic("orders-events", queue) .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) }

A queue name in #[subscriber] long-polls that queue; SqsQueue carries every other setting of the subscription. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the queue orders. The name resolves to the queue's URL through GetQueueUrl once, when the subscription opens. A bare name takes the descriptor's defaults: a 20 second long poll and the queue's own visibility timeout. #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] fixes the kind and leaves the queue to the mount site: b.include(audit.name("audit-eu")) reads audit-eu, so one definition serves several queues. SQS takes only [A-Za-z0-9_-] in a queue name, so every other character of the name becomes - on the way, and a .fifo suffix survives: order.events reads the queue order-events. Two subscriptions on one queue compete for its messages, and each message goes to one of them. A subscription receives at most one batch ahead of its handler. A queue that does not exist stops the service at startup, unless the subscription creates it. Once the service runs, a queue deleted under a subscription ends that subscription, and any other receive error is retried after one second. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and Unnamed<SqsQueue> in place of the name leaves it to name at the mount site.

The queue orders, read with the defaults. A slice handler gets one ReceiveMessage worth of messages; batch(n) becomes MaxNumberOfMessages, capped at ten. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. ReceiveMessage returns several messages per call, so the size becomes its MaxNumberOfMessages and one receive is one batch. Nothing buffers in the service. A batch holds what the queue had at that moment, so a quiet queue yields batches of one. A batch is never empty: a long poll that runs out hands the handler nothing. SQS returns at most ten messages per receive, so a larger size becomes ten, and the subscription logs that once. One outcome settles every message of the batch. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles message i with outcome i. A single-message handler also receives up to ten messages per call, because SQS bills per request, and gets them one at a time; workers(n) decides how many run at once. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acknowledges the batch and Err(outcomes) settles each message.

It /// holds at most the size the mount site names, and as few as one when that is all the queue /// had at the moment of the call. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders-batches"))] async fn reconcile(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "reconciled a batch of orders"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqs_batches.rs /// A batch handler: the slice is one `ReceiveMessage` worth of orders, and `Ok` settles it as a /// whole. create_if_missing() creates the queue at startup when it is missing; a .fifo name creates a FIFO queue, and a dead-letter queue is created too. The subscription calls CreateQueue when it opens and the account does not have the queue yet. Without the step, a missing queue stops the service at startup. A name that ends in .fifo creates a FIFO queue with content-based deduplication. A dead-letter queue the registration declares is created the same way. Every other attribute of a new queue keeps the SQS default, a 30 second visibility timeout among them. The step needs the sqs:CreateQueue permission. It suits a local stack and a test; production queues are usually managed as infrastructure. In process every queue a service names exists already, so the step shows its effect in a live test. The step is on SqsQueue, and on the mount chain through SqsSubscription::create_if_missing, as in the example.

A drafts queue the service opens itself on a fresh stack. A .fifo queue hands out each message group in order and holds a group back while one of its messages is in flight. A queue whose name ends in .fifo is a FIFO queue, and a subscription reads it like any other queue. Every message on it belongs to a message group, which the producer names: the group_id step, the partition key header, or default when it names neither. The queue hands out the messages of a group in the order they were sent. While a message of a group is in flight, the queue holds the rest of that group back until the message is deleted or its visibility lapses. Other groups go on meanwhile. So a retry brings the same message back before the next one of its group. The delivery carries its group in PARTITION_KEY_HEADER. A FIFO queue drops a message whose deduplication id it has seen in the last five minutes. A FIFO queue takes a FIFO dead-letter queue, and create_if_missing on a .fifo name creates a FIFO queue. In process the account keeps the same order and holds a group back the same way.

SqsQueue describes one subscription by queue name or URL, with its long poll, visibility timeout and queue creation. SqsQueue::new takes a queue name or a queue URL (https://sqs...). A name resolves through GetQueueUrl once, when the subscription opens; a URL is used as it is. Three steps set the rest, and each has a default: wait (20 seconds), visibility (the queue's own timeout) and create_if_missing (off). The descriptor goes where the name goes, as the first argument of #[subscriber(..)]. The subscription's name is what the descriptor names: a test reads its deliveries under that name. A descriptor that cannot form a subscription stops the service at startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue, before any call to AWS: an empty name, a wait over 20 seconds, or a visibility outside one second to twelve hours. The same three steps are on the mount chain through SqsSubscription. The manual form builds the descriptor and hands it to the chain with map_source.

Orders read with a ten second long poll, each hidden from other consumers for a minute. Macros Manual examples/sqs_subscriptions_queue.rs /// Reads the queue `orders`: each receive waits up to ten seconds for a message, and a received /// order stays hidden from other consumers for a minute. #[subscriber( SqsQueue::new("orders") .wait(Duration::from_secs(10)) .visibility(Duration::from_secs(60)) )] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(place)) } examples/manual/sqs_subscriptions_queue.rs /// Reads the queue `orders`: each receive waits up to ten seconds for a message, and a received /// order stays hidden from other consumers for a minute. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = SqsQueue::new("orders") .wait(Duration::from_secs(10)) .visibility(Duration::from_secs(60)); b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build().map_source(|_| orders)) }) }

SqsSubscription puts the queue steps on the mount chain, after the framework's own steps such as batch(n) and name. The steps are those of SqsQueue: wait, visibility and create_if_missing. They chain after a framework step: a batch size, a name for a definition that fixed only the kind, or workers(n). A step at the mount site changes the descriptor the attribute built, so it wins over the attribute's value. The steps exist only on the chain of a subscription whose source is an SqsQueue, so they never reach another broker's subscription. The trait comes with the crate's prelude. In the manual form the steps follow map_source or name.

visibility(duration) sets how long a received message stays hidden; the crate re-arms it halfway through each timeout while the handler runs. The visibility timeout is what each receive asks for: how long a received message stays hidden from every other receive. SQS counts the timeout in whole seconds, from one second to twelve hours. A value outside that range stops the service at startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue. A fraction above one second rounds up to the next whole second, so a message never comes back sooner than the timeout asked for. A subscription that names none takes the queue's own timeout, which it reads once with GetQueueAttributes when it opens, so it needs the sqs:GetQueueAttributes permission. A handler may take longer than the timeout. While a handler holds a delivery, the crate re-arms the timeout halfway through each period with ChangeMessageVisibility, so no other consumer receives the message in the meantime. The other half of the period is left for the call to reach the queue, so a one-second timeout is re-armed every half second. SQS keeps a message hidden for at most twelve hours from its receive, and an extension does not restart them. A handler that holds a delivery that long gets one last extension to the end of the twelve hours and a warning in the log; after that the queue hands the message to another consumer. The timeout also decides how soon an abandoned delivery comes back: a message dropped unsettled, or one a stopped process held, is received again once the timeout lapses. In process, a subscription that names no timeout gets the 30 seconds of a new queue; the timeout an operator set on a queue shows only in a live test. The step is on SqsQueue, and on the mount chain through SqsSubscription::visibility, as in the example.

A report takes five seconds to render, and a receive hides it for two; the report is still handled once. The crate /// re-arms the visibility every second while the handler runs, so no other consumer gets the /// report in the meantime. #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn publish_report(report: &Report) -> HandlerOutcome { render(report).await; tracing::info!(report.id, "report published"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( publish_report .name(queue) .visibility(Duration::from_secs(2)), ) }) } examples/manual/sqs_subscriptions_visibility.rs /// Rendering a report takes longer than the two seconds a receive hides it for. The crate /// re-arms the visibility every second while the handler runs, so no other consumer gets the /// report in the meantime. struct PublishReport; impl Handle<Report> for PublishReport { async fn handle( &self, report: &Report, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { render(report).await; tracing::info!(report.id, "report published"); Ok(()) } } fn service(broker: SqsBroker, queue: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<SqsQueue>::new(), PublishReport) .build() .name(queue) .visibility(Duration::from_secs(2)), ) }) }

wait(duration) sets how long one receive waits for a message, 20 seconds by default and at most; a longer wait stops the service at startup. The wait is the WaitTimeSeconds of each ReceiveMessage: the long poll. A receive returns as soon as a message arrives, and returns empty when the wait runs out. An empty receive hands the handler nothing. A longer wait means fewer empty receives, and SQS bills per request. The default is the SQS maximum of 20 seconds, so a subscription that names no wait already polls as long as SQS allows. A wait over 20 seconds stops the service at startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue. A zero wait is short polling: each receive returns at once, with what a sample of the queue's servers holds. The step is on SqsQueue, and on the mount chain through SqsSubscription::wait.

TestApp::start connects SqsBroker to an in-process account with queues, visibility, receive counts, redrive, FIFO groups and topics. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<SqsBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The account has no settings of its own. Its queue URLs are built on the broker's endpoint and region, and every setting a queue has comes from the service's descriptors. Every queue and topic the service names exists in it. The account keeps SQS's semantics. A queue hands each message to one of its subscriptions, and one receive returns at most ten messages. A received message stays invisible until it is deleted or its visibility timeout lapses; a descriptor that names no visibility gets the 30 seconds of a new queue. The receive count rises with every receive, and a redrive policy moves a message whose receives ran out to the dead-letter queue. A FIFO group waits while one of its messages is in flight, and a deduplication id is remembered for five minutes. With sns, a topic delivers a copy to every queue subscribed to it. The account refuses what SQS and SNS refuse: more than ten headers, a header name the service does not take, an empty body or header value, a message over the size limit, a queue name over 80 characters, a dead-letter queue of the other kind, a maxReceiveCount over 1000, a visibility that would end more than twelve hours after the receive, and a FIFO queue on a standard topic. A publish through the harness that SQS would refuse fails the test. A standard queue keeps the order of its messages here, which SQS does not promise. A message sent to a queue no subscription reads is dropped. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled. tb.advance(..), on a clock paused with #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)], moves past a visibility timeout or a deferred retry. What belongs to a running service, such as a queue an operator configured, is for a live test.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } The first test publishes a payment and reads how the handler settled it. TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against LocalStack or AWS, for what belongs to the service: queues, timeouts, credentials. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so every subscription resolves its queue on the stack and every request is signed. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process account leaves to the service: a message kept on a queue no subscription reads, the visibility timeout an operator set on a queue, the queues and topics the service expects to find without creating them, and credentials. A stack keeps what earlier runs left in it, so each run names its queues uniquely, and creates them with create_if_missing or before the app starts. In the example, live::endpoint returns the stack's address from SQS_TEST_ENDPOINT, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no stack. A job that stood a stack up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is LocalStack in docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts.

This guide shows what each handler outcome does to an SQS message, how a handler stays correct when a message arrives twice, and how a batch settles. SQS delivers at least once. A received message stays on the queue, invisible, until the consumer deletes it. A standard queue may also deliver a message twice, and in another order than it was sent (AWS: at-least-once delivery). The example is a payments service that books payments into a ledger and pays refunds.

Every outcome is one SQS call on the message the handler received: Outcome SQS call What happens to the message ack DeleteMessage it leaves the queue drop DeleteMessage it leaves the queue: SQS has no call that rejects a message and keeps it retry ChangeMessageVisibility to zero it is handed out again at once retry_after ChangeMessageVisibility to the delay it is handed out again when the delay ends A message the handler never settles, because the process stopped in the middle, gets no call. It comes back when its visibility timeout ends. So the work of a handler happens before its outcome, and a message is deleted only after the work is done.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a payment on an account under review waits before the next try. const REVIEW: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); /// The receive after which a payment under review is given up. const LAST_RECEIVE: u32 = 3; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments")] struct Payment { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, under_review: bool, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "ledger-entries")] struct Entry { payment: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Entry)] struct Entries; /// The ids of the payments already booked. #[derive(Debug, Default, Clone)] struct Ledger { booked: Arc<Mutex<HashSet<u64>>>, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn book( payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Ledger>, Out(entries): Out<impl Publisher, Entries>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { // SQS counts the receives of a message, this one included. let receives: u32 = ctx .headers() .get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| count.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if payment.under_review { if receives >= LAST_RECEIVE { tracing::error!(payment.id, receives, "payment dropped, still under review"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REVIEW); } let booked = Arc::clone(&ctx.state().booked); if booked .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .contains(&payment.id) { tracing::info!(payment.id, receives, "payment already booked"); return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let entry = Entry { payment: payment.id, account: payment.account.clone(), amount_cents: payment.amount_cents, }; if entries.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { // Nothing is booked yet: the payment comes back and the work runs again. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } booked .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .insert(payment.id); tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// How long a payment on an account under review waits before the next try. const REVIEW: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); /// The receive after which a payment under review is given up. const LAST_RECEIVE: u32 = 3; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payment { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, under_review: bool, } impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Payment { const NAME: &'static str = "Payment"; } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Entry { payment: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Entry { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "ledger-entries"; } impl MessageHeaders for Entry { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Entry { const NAME: &'static str = "Entry"; } struct Entries; impl OutSlot for Entries { const NAME: &'static str = "Entries"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Entries> for Entry {} /// The ids of the payments already booked. #[derive(Debug, Default, Clone)] struct Ledger { booked: Arc<Mutex<HashSet<u64>>>, } struct Book; impl<Wire> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Wire,)>, (), Ledger> for Book where Wire: OutEntry<Entries, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Wire,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Ledger>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { // SQS counts the receives of a message, this one included. let receives: u32 = ctx .headers() .get_str(RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER) .and_then(|count| count.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if payment.under_review { if receives >= LAST_RECEIVE { tracing::error!(payment.id, receives, "payment dropped, still under review"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REVIEW)); } let booked = Arc::clone(&ctx.state().booked); if booked .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .contains(&payment.id) { tracing::info!(payment.id, receives, "payment already booked"); return Ok(()); } let entry = Entry { payment: payment.id, account: payment.account.clone(), amount_cents: payment.amount_cents, }; if outs.get(Entries).message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { // Nothing is booked yet: the payment comes back and the work runs again. return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } booked .lock() .unwrap_or_else(PoisonError::into_inner) .insert(payment.id); tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment booked"); Ok(()) } } book writes a ledger entry for a payment and then acknowledges it. A payment SQS delivers a second time is found among the booked ids and acknowledged without a second entry. The set in the app state stands in for the store a service keeps its booked ids in; the id is the payment's own, not the SQS message id, because a producer that sends twice sends two messages. When the entry cannot be published, nothing is booked, and retry hands the payment back for another try. The handler reads RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER, the queue's own ApproximateReceiveCount. It counts this receive too, so the first delivery reads 1. A payment on an account under review waits a minute with retry_after, and on its third receive the handler gives up and drops it. Retries and dead-letter queues shows how the queue itself caps the receives and keeps what failed.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "refunds")] struct Refund { payment: u64, amount_cents: u64, } /// The largest refund paid without a person's approval. const APPROVAL_LIMIT_CENTS: u64 = 50_000; /// How long a refund waits for approval before it is looked at again. const APPROVAL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(300); /// Settles each refund of a batch on its own: a small refund is paid and deleted, a large one /// waits on the queue for its approval. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("refunds"))] async fn settle_refunds(refunds: &[Refund]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { refunds .iter() .map(|refund| { if refund.amount_cents > APPROVAL_LIMIT_CENTS { tracing::info!(refund.payment, "refund waits for approval"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(APPROVAL) } else { tracing::info!(refund.payment, refund.amount_cents, "refund paid"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } }) .collect() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Refund { payment: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Refund { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "refunds"; } impl MessageHeaders for Refund { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Refund { const NAME: &'static str = "Refund"; } /// The largest refund paid without a person's approval. const APPROVAL_LIMIT_CENTS: u64 = 50_000; /// How long a refund waits for approval before it is looked at again. const APPROVAL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(300); /// Settles each refund of a batch on its own: a small refund is paid and deleted, a large one /// waits on the queue for its approval. struct SettleRefunds; impl Handle<[Refund], (), (), (), Ledger> for SettleRefunds { fn handle( &self, refunds: &[Refund], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Ledger>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let outcomes: Vec<HandlerOutcome> = refunds .iter() .map(|refund| { if refund.amount_cents > APPROVAL_LIMIT_CENTS { tracing::info!(refund.payment, "refund waits for approval"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(APPROVAL) } else { tracing::info!(refund.payment, refund.amount_cents, "refund paid"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } }) .collect(); ready(Err(outcomes)) } } A batch handler returns one outcome per message, in the order of the slice. Each outcome is a call of its own on its message. Here the small refunds are deleted, and a large one stays on the queue and comes back alone after five minutes. A batch handler that returns a single outcome settles every message of the batch with it.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Ledger> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Ledger::default())) .with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include(book) .out(Entries, Publish::default()) .build() .include(settle_refunds.batch(nonzero!(10))) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Ledger> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Ledger::default())) .with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("payments", Book) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("payments")) .build(), ) .out(Entries, Publish::default()) .build() .include( subscriber("refunds", SettleRefunds) .batch(nonzero!(10)) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("refunds")) .build(), ) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } book publishes its entries through the Entries slot, bound to the queue publisher at the mount site. A FIFO queue drops a second send with the same deduplication id for five minutes, which keeps a producer from sending one message twice; FIFO queues shows it. A handler on a standard queue still keeps its own record of what it has done. The tests in the example file deliver a payment twice, let a payment under review run out its receives on a paused clock, and send three refunds in one batch. Testing an SQS service covers the harness.

This guide reads SQS queues: long polling, the visibility timeout of a slow handler, parallel handlers, batches, and one handler on several queues. The example is a warehouse service. It packs orders, books payments and records changes to orders.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, items: u32, } /// Packs an order. Packing takes up to a minute, so each receive asks for a minute of /// visibility, and four orders are packed at once. #[subscriber( SqsQueue::new("orders") .visibility(Duration::from_secs(60)) .create_if_missing(), workers(4) )] async fn pack(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order packed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, items: u32, } impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Order { const NAME: &'static str = "Order"; } /// Packs an order. struct Pack; impl Handle<Order> for Pack { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order packed"); ready(Ok(())) } } A subscription long-polls its queue with ReceiveMessage. Each call waits up to 20 seconds for a message, the most SQS allows. wait sets a shorter wait. A queue is named by its name or by its URL, and a name is resolved with GetQueueUrl once, at startup. A single-message subscription still asks for up to ten messages per call, because SQS bills per request. It hands them to the handler one at a time. A background task receives the next batch while the handler works, and it never runs more than one batch ahead.
documents.s: A queue and its long poll

documents.t: A received message stays invisible to other consumers for the queue's visibility timeout. If it is not deleted by then, SQS hands it out again. visibility asks for a timeout of its own on each receive, between one second and twelve hours. SQS counts it in whole seconds, so a fraction rounds up to the next second. pack asks for a minute. Without the step, the subscription reads the queue's own timeout once, when it opens. A handler may run longer than the timeout. While a delivery is alive, the crate extends its visibility halfway through each timeout, so a slow handler does not see its message handed to another consumer. SQS keeps a message hidden for at most twelve hours from its receive. A handler that runs that long gets one last extension to the end of them and a warning in the log, and the message then goes to another consumer.

workers(4) runs up to four deliveries of orders at once. The four handlers share the messages each receive returns. A standard queue has no order to keep, so nothing else is needed. FIFO queues keep one message group in order with workers(n, by_key).

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments")] struct Payment { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, } /// Books the payments one receive returned, in one write to the ledger. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("payments"))] async fn reconcile(payments: &[Payment]) -> HandlerOutcome { let total: u64 = payments.iter().map(|payment| payment.amount_cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = payments.len(), total, "payments booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payment { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Payment { const NAME: &'static str = "Payment"; } /// Books the payments one receive returned, in one write to the ledger. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Payment]> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let total: u64 = payments.iter().map(|payment| payment.amount_cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = payments.len(), total, "payments booked"); ready(Ok(())) } } A handler that takes a slice is a batch handler. The size its mount site names becomes MaxNumberOfMessages, so one receive is one batch. A batch holds what the queue had at the time, and a long poll that returns nothing yields no batch. ReceiveMessage returns at most ten messages, so a larger size is lowered to ten and the service logs it once. Each message of a batch is settled on its own; Acknowledgement shows the outcomes.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Change { order: u64, by: String, } /// Records a change to an order. The definition fixes the kind of queue and leaves its name /// to the mount site. #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] async fn audit(change: &Change) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(change.order, change.by, "change recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Change { order: u64, by: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Change { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Change { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Change { const NAME: &'static str = "Change"; } /// Records a change to an order, on whichever queue it is mounted. struct Audit; impl Handle<Change> for Audit { fn handle( &self, change: &Change, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(change.order, change.by, "change recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } #[subscriber(SqsQueue)] fixes the kind of source and leaves the queue's name open. The mount site names it with .name(..), once per queue.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include(pack) // Up to ten payments per call: one receive is one batch. .include( reconcile .batch(nonzero!(10)) .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)) .create_if_missing(), ) // One definition, two queues. .include(audit.name("audit-eu").create_if_missing()) .include(audit.name("audit-us").create_if_missing()) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { let audit = |queue: &'static str| { subscriber(queue, Audit) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new(queue).create_if_missing()) .build() }; // A minute of visibility per receive, four orders packed at once. b.include( subscriber("orders", Pack) .map_source(|_| { SqsQueue::new("orders") .visibility(Duration::from_secs(60)) .create_if_missing() }) .workers(nonzero!(4)) .build(), ) // Up to ten payments per call: one receive is one batch. .include( subscriber("payments", Reconcile) .batch(nonzero!(10)) .map_source(|_| { SqsQueue::new("payments") .wait(Duration::from_secs(20)) .create_if_missing() }) .build(), ) // One handler, two queues. .include(audit("audit-eu")) .include(audit("audit-us")) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The queue steps also sit at the mount site, after the framework's own steps, through SqsSubscription. An empty queue name, a wait over 20 seconds or a visibility outside its range stops the service at startup with SqsError::InvalidQueue, before any call to AWS. A name may hold characters SQS does not take: each character outside A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ and - becomes -, and a .fifo suffix is kept. create_if_missing creates a queue that does not exist. A production service usually takes its queues from its infrastructure and leaves the step out; a missing queue then stops it at startup.

Each message attribute arrives as a header, and each header of a publish leaves as an attribute. Two headers are the crate's own. RECEIVE_COUNT_HEADER carries the queue's receive count of the message. PARTITION_KEY_HEADER carries the message group of a FIFO queue. An SQS body is text, so a binary payload travels base64-encoded with a marker attribute and arrives decoded. Base64 makes such a payload a third larger, and SQS refuses a message over its size limit. The tests in the example file publish orders, payments and changes to the app in process. Testing an SQS service covers the harness.

This guide publishes a message to an SNS topic once and lets SNS deliver a copy to every SQS queue subscribed to the topic. SNS to SQS is how AWS services fan out: one topic, one queue per consumer. The crate publishes to topics; each queue behind a topic is read the ordinary way. Publishing to SNS needs the sns feature: Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.8", features = ["sns"] } The example is a shop. It accepts an order and announces it on a topic, and billing and shipping each read the announcement from a queue of their own.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shop-orders")] struct PlaceOrder { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } /// The announcement names the topic, so the handler answers with a bare `reply` clause. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shop-order-events")] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("shop-orders").create_if_missing(), reply)] async fn accept(order: &PlaceOrder) -> OrderPlaced { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); OrderPlaced { id: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct PlaceOrder { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for PlaceOrder { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "shop-orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for PlaceOrder { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for PlaceOrder { const NAME: &'static str = "PlaceOrder"; } /// The announcement names the topic it is published to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct OrderPlaced { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for OrderPlaced { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "shop-order-events"; } impl MessageHeaders for OrderPlaced { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for OrderPlaced { const NAME: &'static str = "OrderPlaced"; } struct Accept; impl Handle<PlaceOrder, OrderPlaced> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &PlaceOrder, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderPlaced, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); ready(Ok(OrderPlaced { id: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, })) } } accept answers each order with an OrderPlaced, and the type names where it goes: shop-order-events. The mount site decides whether that name is a queue or a topic.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("shop-billing").create_if_missing())] async fn bill(order: &OrderPlaced) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("shop-shipping").create_if_missing())] async fn ship(order: &OrderPlaced) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Bill; impl Handle<OrderPlaced> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Ship; impl Handle<OrderPlaced> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } bill and ship are ordinary queue handlers. Each queue gets its own copy of every announcement, so billing and shipping work at their own pace and retry on their own.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Subscribes the billing and shipping queues to the topic, with raw delivery. /// /// `broker` is a clone of the app's broker, so it uses the connection the app already holds. async fn subscribe_queues(broker: SqsBroker) -> io::Result<()> { let connected = broker.connect().await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; for queue in ["shop-billing", "shop-shipping"] { connected .subscribe_queue_to_topic("shop-order-events", queue) .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) } src/main.rs /// Subscribes the billing and shipping queues to the topic, with raw delivery. /// /// `broker` is a clone of the app's broker, so it uses the connection the app already holds. async fn subscribe_queues(broker: SqsBroker) -> io::Result<()> { let connected = broker.connect().await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; for queue in ["shop-billing", "shop-shipping"] { connected .subscribe_queue_to_topic("shop-order-events", queue) .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; } Ok(()) } subscribe_queue_to_topic subscribes a queue to a topic with raw message delivery. So a copy arrives as a plain SQS message: the payload is the body, and each header is a message attribute. Without raw delivery SNS would wrap the message in a JSON envelope of its own. SNS delivers to a queue only when the queue's access policy lets the topic send to it. The call adds that statement to the policy before it subscribes, and keeps the statements already there. The call creates the topic when it does not exist, and subscribing the same queue again changes nothing. Topology is usually infrastructure, created with Terraform or the console. Here a startup hook does it on a clone of the app's broker, which uses the connection the app already holds.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> RustStream { let topology = broker.clone(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")) .after_startup(async move |_state| subscribe_queues(topology).await) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // The reply goes to the topic named by `OrderPlaced`, through SNS. b.include(accept) .out_reply(SnsPublish::default()) .include(bill) .include(ship) }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: SqsBroker) -> RustStream { let topology = broker.clone(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")) .after_startup(async move |_state| subscribe_queues(topology).await) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // The reply goes to the topic named by `OrderPlaced`, through SNS. b.include( subscriber("shop-orders", Accept) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("shop-orders").create_if_missing()) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(SnsPublish::default()) .include( subscriber("shop-billing", Bill) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("shop-billing").create_if_missing()) .build(), ) .include( subscriber("shop-shipping", Ship) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("shop-shipping").create_if_missing()) .build(), ) }) } fn app() -> RustStream { service( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } .out_reply(SnsPublish::default()) binds the reply to SnsPublish, and the reply becomes an SNS Publish to the topic. Without that step the same reply rides the broker's default policy, SqsPublish, and lands on a queue named shop-order-events. SnsPublish opens a topic by name with CreateTopic, which returns the existing topic when there is one, or takes the topic's ARN as the name. The same policy works in an Out slot and in a startup hook, and ConnectedSqsBroker::sns_publisher gives a publisher outside the app. A topic whose name ends in .fifo is a FIFO topic. It carries the message group of a publish to the FIFO queues subscribed to it, with the group steps a FIFO queue takes. A FIFO queue subscribes only to a FIFO topic. The service needs sns:CreateTopic and sns:Publish to publish. To subscribe queues itself it also needs sns:Subscribe on the topic and sqs:GetQueueAttributes and sqs:SetQueueAttributes on each queue.

The example file runs one test body twice. In process, the in-process account delivers a topic's messages to the queues subscribed with subscribe_queue_to_topic, so the hook wires the test as it wires production. A queue an operator subscribed outside the service is named on the policy with fans_out_to, a step of the testing feature. With SQS_TEST_ENDPOINT set, the same body runs against LocalStack through TestApp::start_live: cargo test --features sns SQS_TEST_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4566 cargo test --features sns -- --test-threads=1 Testing an SQS service covers the harness and the live mode.

This guide sends to an SQS FIFO queue in message groups, drops duplicate sends with a deduplication id, and handles several groups at once, each in order. A FIFO queue keeps the order of the messages within a message group and hands out a group's next message only after the one before it is deleted. Each send also carries a deduplication id, and the queue drops a second send with the same id for five minutes (AWS: deduplication). A queue whose name ends in .fifo is a FIFO queue. The example is a shipping service. It turns each order into a shipment, and the shipments of one customer go out in the order the customer placed them.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, customer: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments.fifo")] struct Shipment { order: u64, customer: String, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders").create_if_missing())] async fn dispatch( order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = Shipment { order: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; // A customer's shipments form one group, so they are handled in the order they were sent. // The order id is the deduplication id, so sending the same order again ships nothing more. let sent = shipments .message(&shipment) .group_id(&order.customer) .deduplication_id(order.id.to_string()) .publish() .await; if sent.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, customer: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Order { const NAME: &'static str = "Order"; } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Shipment { order: u64, customer: String, } impl OutgoingDestination for Shipment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "shipments.fifo"; } impl MessageHeaders for Shipment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Shipment { const NAME: &'static str = "Shipment"; } struct Shipments; impl OutSlot for Shipments { const NAME: &'static str = "Shipments"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Shipments> for Shipment {} struct Dispatch; impl<Wire> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Wire,)>> for Dispatch where Wire: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher<Options = SqsPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Wire,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = Shipment { order: order.id, customer: order.customer.clone(), }; // A customer's shipments form one group, so they are handled in the order they were // sent. The order id is the deduplication id, so sending the same order again ships // nothing more. let sent = outs .get(Shipments) .message(&shipment) .group_id(&order.customer) .deduplication_id(order.id.to_string()) .publish() .await; if sent.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } dispatch publishes a shipment to shipments.fifo through the Shipments slot. The slot is bounded on SqsPublishOptions, so the publish takes the steps of SqsPublishSteps. A handler that names these steps imports this crate's prelude. group_id puts the shipment in the customer's group. When a publish names no group, the group comes from the message's PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, then from the group the policy fixed with Publish::default().group_id(..), and last it is "default". The header is the spelling every RustStream broker reads, so a producer that sets it needs no SQS step. deduplication_id is the order's id. When orders delivers an order twice, the second shipment is a send the queue drops. A publish that names no deduplication id gets an id unique to the process, so two equal payloads sent on purpose both arrive. A policy carries no deduplication id: one fixed id would drop every send after the first. A group or a deduplication id on a standard queue is refused with SqsError::NotFifo.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Ships one shipment. Four groups are handled at once, each group in its own order. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("shipments.fifo").create_if_missing(), workers(4, by_key))] async fn ship(shipment: &Shipment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let group = ctx .headers() .get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(shipment.order, group, "shipment sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Ships one shipment. struct Ship; impl Handle<Shipment> for Ship { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let group = ctx .headers() .get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(shipment.order, group, "shipment sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } A delivery from a FIFO queue carries its group in PARTITION_KEY_HEADER. workers(4, by_key) runs four lanes and sends every message of one group to the same lane. So four customers ship at once, and the shipments of one customer go out one after another. One receive can return several messages of a group, and plain workers(4) would run them side by side.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include(dispatch) .out(Shipments, Publish::default()) .build() .include(ship) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Dispatch) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("orders").create_if_missing()) .build(), ) .out(Shipments, Publish::default()) .build() // Four groups at once, each group in its own order. .include( subscriber("shipments.fifo", Ship) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("shipments.fifo").create_if_missing()) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)) .build(), ) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } create_if_missing creates shipments.fifo as a FIFO queue with content-based deduplication. A FIFO queue takes a FIFO dead-letter queue; Retries and dead-letter queues covers the cap. SQS limits the throughput of one group, so a service spreads its load over many groups. The tests in the example file check the group a shipment travels in, send one order twice, and send the orders of two customers at once. Testing an SQS service covers the harness.
This guide installs ruststream-sqs-sns, starts a local SQS and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.8", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-sqs-sns = "0.8" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-sqs-sns = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-sqs-sns is the SQS broker, built on the official aws-sdk-sqs client. Its testing feature adds the in-process SQS that tests run on. The broker crate has these features, all off by default: Feature What it gives sns publishing to SNS topics with SnsPublish, over aws-sdk-sns (Fan-out with SNS) asyncapi the sqs and sns bindings in the generated AsyncAPI document testing the in-process SQS behind TestApp

LocalStack runs SQS and SNS in one container: compose.yaml services: localstack: image: localstack/localstack:4.14.0 ports: - "4566:4566" environment: SERVICES: sqs,sns SQS_ENDPOINT_STRATEGY: path docker compose up -d The stack answers on http://localhost:4566 and starts with no queues.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } // The local stack starts empty, so the descriptor creates the queue on subscribe. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders").create_if_missing())] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| b.include(take_order), ) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { // The local stack starts empty, so the descriptor creates the queue on subscribe. b.include( subscriber("orders", TakeOrder) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("orders").create_if_missing()) .build(), ) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders from the orders queue. It acknowledges an order with an amount and drops one without. SqsQueue names the queue, and create_if_missing creates it when the subscription opens. A production service leaves that step out and takes its queues from its infrastructure. SqsBroker::new only records the configuration. endpoint, region and test_credentials point it at the local stack. The SDK clients are built when the service starts. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run Send an order from another terminal with the AWS CLI: export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566 AWS_REGION=us-east-1 \ AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test aws sqs send-message \ --queue-url "$(aws sqs get-queue-url --queue-name orders --output text)" \ --message-body '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' The service logs order taken with the order's id. Ctrl+C stops it.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. SqsBroker connects to an in-process SQS there, so the tests need no stack: cargo test Testing an SQS service walks through these tests and what the in-process SQS models.

A service on aws-sdk-sqs writes its own receive loop. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: aws-sdk-sqs RustStream aws_config::load_from_env and Client::new SqsBroker::new, or SqsBroker::from_config with an SdkConfig of your own (Running in production) get_queue_url the queue name in SqsQueue::new, resolved once at startup a receive_message().wait_time_seconds(20) loop a #[subscriber] handler (Consuming queues) deserializing message.body() the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec delete_message after the work the handler's outcome, HandlerOutcome::ack (Acknowledgement and delivery guarantees) change_message_visibility HandlerOutcome::retry_after (Retries and dead-letter queues) a RedrivePolicy set in the console max_attempts and dead_letter at the mount site send_message a reply or an Out parameter, sent through SqsPublish message_group_id and message_deduplication_id the publish steps group_id and deduplication_id (FIFO queues)
This guide runs an SQS service on AWS: where its credentials and region come from, the timeouts it runs with, and the IAM permissions it needs.

SqsBroker::new() takes nothing from the code. The AWS SDK's default chain finds the region and the credentials when the service starts: environment variables, the shared ~/.aws files, SSO, and the role of the container or the instance. A service that runs under an IAM role on ECS, EKS, Lambda or EC2 needs no configuration at all. The SDK reads credentials when it signs its first request. That request is the GetQueueUrl of the first subscription, at startup, so a service with wrong credentials stops before it handles a message.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The AWS configuration of the service: a pinned behaviour version, its region, the /// credentials of the `orders-service` profile, read when the first request is signed, and a /// request timeout above the 20 seconds a long poll waits. fn aws_config() -> SdkConfig { let credentials = ProfileFileCredentialsProvider::builder() .profile_name("orders-service") .build(); SdkConfig::builder() .behavior_version(BehaviorVersion::v2026_01_12()) .region(Region::new("eu-west-1")) .credentials_provider(SharedCredentialsProvider::new(credentials)) .timeout_config( TimeoutConfig::builder() .operation_attempt_timeout(Duration::from_secs(25)) .build(), ) .build() } src/main.rs /// The AWS configuration of the service: a pinned behaviour version, its region, the /// credentials of the `orders-service` profile, read when the first request is signed, and a /// request timeout above the 20 seconds a long poll waits. fn aws_config() -> SdkConfig { let credentials = ProfileFileCredentialsProvider::builder() .profile_name("orders-service") .build(); SdkConfig::builder() .behavior_version(BehaviorVersion::v2026_01_12()) .region(Region::new("eu-west-1")) .credentials_provider(SharedCredentialsProvider::new(credentials)) .timeout_config( TimeoutConfig::builder() .operation_attempt_timeout(Duration::from_secs(25)) .build(), ) .build() } SqsBroker::from_config takes an SdkConfig the service builds. aws_config builds one from the environment with an async loader, while the app function is synchronous. So the example builds it with SdkConfig::builder(), which does no I/O. The profile provider reads the orders-service profile on the first request; a profile with a role_arn assumes that role. The pinned behaviour version keeps the SDK's defaults from changing under the service when the SDK is updated. The configuration also carries the request timeout described below: the broker keeps every setting of the configuration except an endpoint or a region named on the broker itself. The example needs two more dependencies: Cargo.toml [dependencies] aws-config = "1" aws-sdk-sqs = "1"

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } // The queue belongs to the infrastructure, so the descriptor does not create it. It names its // visibility, so the subscription does not read the queue's own. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("orders").visibility(Duration::from_secs(120)))] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(SqsBroker::from_config(aws_config()), |b| { b.include(take_order) }) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Order { const NAME: &'static str = "Order"; } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::from_config(aws_config()), |b| { // The queue belongs to the infrastructure, so the descriptor does not create it. It // names its visibility, so the subscription does not read the queue's own. b.include( subscriber("orders", TakeOrder) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("orders").visibility(Duration::from_secs(120))) .build(), ) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The orders queue belongs to the infrastructure: Terraform, CloudFormation or the console create it, with its redrive policy and encryption. The descriptor leaves out create_if_missing, so a missing queue stops the service at startup instead of creating an empty one. It names its visibility, so the subscription does not read the queue's own timeout. endpoint and region point the broker at another endpoint, a VPC endpoint or a local stack. On a broker built with from_config they replace the configuration's own endpoint_url and region. The queue URLs SQS returns are rebased onto the endpoint.

SqsBroker::new() gives each SQS request 25 seconds per attempt, above the 20 seconds a long poll may wait. A configuration of your own sets this with timeout_config, as the example does; an attempt timeout under 20 seconds would end every long poll. The SDK retries a failed request with its own retry policy. Requests go over the SDK's default HTTPS client. A handler on a dedicated thread (threads(n)) sends through SDK clients of its own, built from the same configuration and sharing its credentials.

The service above needs these permissions on its queue: policy.json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "sqs:GetQueueUrl", "sqs:ReceiveMessage", "sqs:DeleteMessage", "sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:eu-west-1:123456789012:orders" } ] } Each feature adds its own: Feature Permissions a subscription that names no visibility sqs:GetQueueAttributes on the queue max_attempts and dead_letter sqs:SetQueueAttributes on the queue, sqs:GetQueueAttributes on the dead-letter queue create_if_missing sqs:CreateQueue a publish to a queue sqs:GetQueueUrl and sqs:SendMessage on the queue a publish to a topic sns:CreateTopic and sns:Publish on the topic subscribe_queue_to_topic sns:CreateTopic and sns:Subscribe on the topic, sqs:GetQueueUrl, sqs:GetQueueAttributes and sqs:SetQueueAttributes on the queue

With the asyncapi feature, the service's AsyncAPI document names one server: the host of the broker's endpoint, or else the regional host of its region, such as sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com. The document never holds a credential or a queue's ARN, so it can be published. The tests in the example file start the same app in process; the in-process SQS takes the region from the configuration and signs nothing. Testing an SQS service covers the harness.

This guide retries an SQS message now or later, caps its deliveries and lets SQS move what keeps failing to a dead-letter queue. SQS does both jobs itself. A retry is the same message made visible again, with its receive count intact. The cap and the dead-letter queue are the queue's redrive policy, and the mount site declares it. The example is an invoices service that charges invoices to customers.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The largest invoice charged without a credit check. const CREDIT_LIMIT_CENTS: u64 = 100_000; /// How long an invoice waits for the credit check before it comes back. const CREDIT_CHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "invoices")] struct Invoice { id: u64, customer: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("invoices").create_if_missing())] async fn charge(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { if invoice.customer.is_empty() { // Another try gets the same answer. tracing::warn!(invoice.id, "invoice without a customer dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if invoice.amount_cents > CREDIT_LIMIT_CENTS { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice waits for the credit check"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(CREDIT_CHECK); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, invoice.amount_cents, "invoice charged"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// The largest invoice charged without a credit check. const CREDIT_LIMIT_CENTS: u64 = 100_000; /// How long an invoice waits for the credit check before it comes back. const CREDIT_CHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Invoice { id: u64, customer: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Invoice { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "invoices"; } impl MessageHeaders for Invoice { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Invoice { const NAME: &'static str = "Invoice"; } struct Charge; impl Handle<Invoice> for Charge { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if invoice.customer.is_empty() { // Another try gets the same answer. tracing::warn!(invoice.id, "invoice without a customer dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } if invoice.amount_cents > CREDIT_LIMIT_CENTS { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice waits for the credit check"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(CREDIT_CHECK))); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, invoice.amount_cents, "invoice charged"); ready(Ok(())) } } An invoice over the credit limit waits for a credit check. retry_after sets the message's visibility timeout to 30 seconds, and SQS hands it out again when they end. SQS counts whole seconds, so a fraction of a second rounds up. SQS keeps a message hidden for at most twelve hours from its receive, so a delay ends within them. A longer delay is shortened to end with them, and the crate logs a warning that names the queue. The message stays on its queue the whole time, so a deferred retry survives a restart of the service. retry sets the visibility to zero, and the message is handed out again at once. An invoice without a customer gets the same answer on every try, so charge drops it.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoices", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { // Four deliveries of one invoice, the first included; then SQS moves it. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(4u32)) .dead_letter("invoices-dead") .include(review) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoices", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqsBroker::new() .endpoint("http://localhost:4566") .region("us-east-1") .test_credentials(), |b| { // Four deliveries of one invoice, the first included; then SQS moves it. b.include( subscriber("invoices", Charge) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("invoices").create_if_missing()) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(4u32)) .dead_letter("invoices-dead") .include( subscriber("invoices-dead", Review) .map_source(|_| SqsQueue::new("invoices-dead").create_if_missing()) .build(), ) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts and dead_letter together are the queue's redrive policy. The cap becomes its maxReceiveCount, and the dead-letter queue becomes its target. The subscription writes the policy onto the queue when it opens. From then on SQS counts the receives and moves a message that ran out of them; the service publishes nothing. Here an invoice is delivered four times, and on the fifth receive SQS moves it to invoices-dead. The two steps go together. A cap without a dead-letter queue, or a dead-letter queue without a cap, stops the service at startup with SqsError::IncompleteRedrive, which names the missing half. SQS takes a maxReceiveCount of at most 1000. The dead-letter queue must exist when the subscription opens, unless a descriptor of the app creates it with create_if_missing. It must be of the same kind as its queue: a FIFO queue takes a FIFO dead-letter queue. Writing the policy needs sqs:SetQueueAttributes on the queue and sqs:GetQueueAttributes on the dead-letter queue. drop deletes a message. On a capped queue, a drop of the delivery that used up the last receive returns the message instead, so SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue rather than losing it.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Reads the invoices SQS moved away after their last delivery. #[subscriber(SqsQueue::new("invoices-dead").create_if_missing())] async fn review(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(invoice.id, invoice.customer, "invoice needs a review"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Reads the invoices SQS moved away after their last delivery. struct Review; impl Handle<Invoice> for Review { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!(invoice.id, invoice.customer, "invoice needs a review"); ready(Ok(())) } } A dead-letter queue is an ordinary queue, and review reads it like any other. The message arrives as it was sent, with its attributes. A queue with no reader keeps its messages until its retention period ends, so a person can also look at them in the console.

The tests in the example file run the app in process with a paused clock, so tb.advance(CREDIT_CHECK) lets the 30 seconds pass at once. One test runs an invoice through its four deliveries into invoices-dead, another checks that a cap without a dead-letter queue does not start. Testing an SQS service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process SQS or against a running stack. The service under test is a checkout. An order arrives on checkout-orders, and confirm answers it with a confirmation on checkout-confirmations, which notify reads. An order without an amount is dropped. A back-ordered order waits an hour with retry_after and comes back to be checked again. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-sqs-sns in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_is_confirmed() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(SqsBroker::new())).await?; a_confirmation_follows_the_order(tb).await } async fn a_confirmation_follows_the_order(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<SqsBroker>() .message(&order(1, 2_500, false)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<SqsBroker>() .subscriber("checkout-orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&order(1, 2_500, false)) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<SqsBroker>() .subscriber("checkout-confirmations") .assert_called_once() .with(&Confirmation { order: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_order_is_confirmed() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(SqsBroker::new())).await?; a_confirmation_follows_the_order(tb).await } async fn a_confirmation_follows_the_order(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<SqsBroker>() .message(&order(1, 2_500, false)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<SqsBroker>() .subscriber("checkout-orders") .assert_called_once() .with(&order(1, 2_500, false)) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<SqsBroker>() .subscriber("checkout-confirmations") .assert_called_once() .with(&Confirmation { order: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects SqsBroker to an in-process SQS. No endpoint is called and no credentials are needed. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<SqsBroker>(). publish returns once the handlers it reached have settled, the reply and its reader included. So the next lines assert on finished state: how confirm settled the order and what notify received. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

An hour of RESTOCK costs nothing. retry_after makes the message invisible for the delay, as SQS does, and the queue hands it out again when the clock passes it. published shows one order on checkout-orders: the second delivery is the same message, not a copy.

documents.t: The in-process SQS is an account inside the test, and every queue and topic the service names exists in it. It models what a service's logic depends on: A queue hands each message to one of its subscriptions, and a received message stays invisible until it is deleted or its visibility timeout ends. The receive count grows with every receive, and a redrive policy moves a message whose receives ran out to the dead-letter queue. A batch holds at most the ten messages one receive returns. A FIFO group waits while one of its messages is in flight, and a deduplication id is remembered for five minutes. With sns, a topic delivers a copy to every queue subscribed with subscribe_queue_to_topic. What SQS or SNS refuses is refused there too: more than ten headers, a header name SQS does not take, an empty body or header value, a message over the size limit, a queue name over 80 characters, a dead-letter queue of the other kind, a maxReceiveCount over 1000, a visibility that would end more than twelve hours after the receive, and a FIFO queue on a standard topic. A standard queue keeps the order of its messages there, which SQS does not promise. A descriptor that names no visibility gets 30 seconds, the default of a new queue. A message sent to a queue no subscription reads is dropped. The visibility an operator set on a queue, the queues and topics the service expects to find, and credentials are exercised against a running stack.
